From the St. Lucia Palladium, July 3. A ppeara nee of Choi c ia . The much dreaded disease known as Cholera, has made its appearance amongst us ; one solitary case arising out

last, proved fatal the next day. The individual, it appears, had gorged himself on putrid meat taken from a dead ox which had been thrown in the sea from the schooner Contractor , and then having stimulated himself with strong drink, went to sleep under one of'the balconies, the bricks of the pavement on which he laid being saturated by the heavy rains; during the night he was attacked with violent cramps and diarrhoea, which eventually terminated according to medical authority, in a confirmed case of cholera. Some short time since, an aggravated case of diarrhoea of which the i patient died, produced a fearful panic among the people of this Town ; one could scarcely be met with whose unquiet looks and fear stricken visage did not give signs of the restless workings of a perturbed mind under expectation of some dreadful calamity; now the case

not with that apprehension which seems to be the forerunner of some terrible catastrophe. This is owing to the acts of the Corporation, and the vigorous steps taken by the Authorities ; and now that þÿmen m s inds are calmed, and confidence restored, things will go on well, and there will be less risk of witnessing here those harrowing scenes which cholera so lately produced in Barbados. A new burial ground has been opened by the Government at a distance from Town, in a westerly direction near to Vieille Ville, and the first cholera victim has been interred there; immediately after death the man was removed, and the house in which he died, white-washed with lime. The Town is parcelled out into Medical Districts, and house to house visitors are being named to report daily the health of each locality, so that no case can occur without its being immediately known. In consequence of the schooner Greyhound being suffered, contrary to the published notification of the Acting Colonial Secretary, to enter the harbour without being first visited by the Health Officer, and landing her sick captain, who fortunately was attacked with dy-

sentery, and not cholera, orders have been given to the Tapion battery to fire on any vessel attempting to enter the harbour, unless being first boarded by the Harbour Master, to whom, by the bye, the fault of the Greyhound breaking through the harbour rules, is to be attributed.

In addition to the intelligence contained in our files from Barbados which the Steamer brought on the 28th ultimo, we find through the means of a private let- 1 ter received here, that up to the 20th of June, (5,(561 cases of Cholera have proved fatal. The letter informs us that þÿ þÿ The disease is certainly on the decline as far as regards the City, but it is increasing in all the Country Parishes. At least two-thirds of the interments reported for the City since 19th and 20th June, are from the rural parts of the Parish. As the numbers become less, the virulence seems to be increased. The disease is not so rife among the lower classes just now, but it seems to attack now the middling and higher classes. It is impossible to state with j any accuracy either, which has been the most successful mode of treatment, or the number of cases treated, as no correct account has been kept. The exact mortality will never be ascertained, as in the country, persons are interring their friends in their own lands, whilst in this City in many instances one coffin contains the parent and child or , þÿchildren. Many of our Sister-Colonies have pas- ! sed quarantine regulations, in Grenada, seven days from Barbados are allowed ; St. Vincent, 14 days from Barbados, and through the kindness of a gentleman in town, we find that in Demerara 40 days quarantine are exacted before any vessel from Barbados would be allowed to pratique. We are indebted to the same gentleman for the following intelligence

respecting the New York line of Steamers to St. Thomas. We take the extract from a letter dated Philadelphia, June 1st, 1854, the writer says þÿ þÿ We would call your attention to the i fact that the Steamer Curlew which has been carrying the mails from New York to St. Thomas, has been withdrawn from the route, and her Agent announces that the line will be discontinued for the þÿfuture.

The 9th meeting of the Council was held on 23rd J uly 1 1 þÿo clock At the final discussion of the draft regarding the reorganisation of the Upper Court, the Vice Chairman again took over the functions of the Chairman. An amendment of minor consequence proposed by the Governor having been agreed to, the draft was accepted with a majority of 15 votes against 2 . The þÿCouncil report s to H. M. the King will henceforth be produced. The Council next proceeded to the first discussion of the following three drafts : 1 , Draft of an ordinance concerning taxes in in the island of St. Thomas to the LaudtrCasury. The report of the Committee was explained and supported by the Reporter þÿ Mr. Stencrsen, þÿ and several amendments were proposed principally by Messrs. Birch and Hanschell. 2, Draft of an ordinance concerning taxes in the island of St. Croix to the Landtreasury. The reporter þÿ Mr Arnesen þÿ endeavored to substantiate the proposal of the Committee, that the additional duty mentioned in 1 should also be levied in the import duties, which was seconded by Mr. þÿMc Cutchin. Mr. Birch proposed a modification of the provisions relative to the Absentee-tax, to be adopted in the draft 3, Draft of an ordinance concerning the Building-tax ordained by the law of 1st October 1802. Mr. þÿMc Cutchin proposed, that the so termed negro-houses, when occupied by servants employed by the owners or the renters should be exempted from paying this tax The meeting was adjourned at 3 þÿo clock

Tho 10th meeting of the Council was held Thursday the 6th of July at 11 þÿo clock Mr. Castonier was absent. The Chairman notified, that he had received from the 2nd member for Frederiksted þÿ Mr Newtonþÿ draft of a law for raising funds by the Landtreasury of St. Croix to defray the expenses attending the importation of laborers from foreign places The Council then proceeded to the final discussion of

s 1 , Draft of an ordinance concerning taxes to the Landtreasury of St. Thomas. 2, Draft of an ordinance concerning taxes to the Landtreasury of St. Croix. 3, Draft of an ordinance concerning the Building-tax ordained by the law of first October 1802. The result of these discussions will be known from the reports to H. M. the King, which will henceforth be printed. The meeting was adjourned at 4 j þÿo clock.

The 11th meeting of the Council was held Monday the 10th ot July at 11 þÿo clock. Mr. Castonier was absent. The draft of law prohibiting foreign lotteries in these Colonies was put to the first discussion. The Governor having expressed his opinion with regard to the report of the Committee and especially explained, that the Committee had in the report only taken notice of sellers of lottery tickets, while the intention of the draft is also that of procuring a counterpoise against the sale of them, the report of the Committee was defended bv the reporter þÿ Mr. Arnesen, whereafter Messrs. Birch, Hanschell, Hawley and De Gout partook of the discussion. The final report on the draft of an ordinance relative to Commerce and Shipping in St Thomas was read. Finally the draft of a law for raising means for defraying the expenses attending the importation of foreign laborers was produced. The mover þÿ Mr. Newton explained fully the urgent necessity of the proposed institution and based the same on statistical statements, which went to show an annual decrease of the number of laborers. The total number of laborers were : in the year 1841 ------ - - - - - 15,328 16,632 in the year 1846 ------ 13,745 in the year 1850 ------ 13,201 in the year 1S52 in the year 1853 ------ 12,865 thus in 12 years the number was reduced with 4000 individuals, besides deducting from the present number about 3000 able laborers ; he subsequently pointed out, that the want of labor has caused, that the present crop, in spite of the

favorable weather, was only a middling one, about 12000 hogsheads, whilst it in case the same force was available as in the year 1846 and 1847, without doubt would have amounted to 20,000 hogsheads, so that the Absentee-tax alone would have been sufficient to cover the deficiency of the Landtreasury, without imposing new taxes. This rotrogradation had taken place notwithstanding the planters had spared neither trouble nor expense in order to make up for the wanting force of labor by machinery and cattle, and by improved agriculture. He finally proposed the appointment of a Committee of 5 members, which proposal was seconded by Mr. Christmas. During the succeeding discussion of the matter, this proposal was recommended by Messrs. Me.'Cutchiu, Hcilbuth, Birch, Arnesen and Burt. The appointment of a Committee having been agreed upon, the following members were elected : Messrs: Newton with 14 votes Birch with 14 þÿ Arnesen with 13 þÿ Hailbuth with 12 þÿ and a re-election, in consequence of a division of votes Burt with 9 votes. The meeting was adjourned at 3 þÿo clock.

QSOIZ A 7 1 3. which the dreadful Epidemic of Asiatic Cholera maintains its hold, under any circumstances, no one we are sure who read the account we published a fortnight ago of the ravages it was making here, was so sanguine us to expect that the succeeding budget of news hencewnrd would unfold tho gratifying intelligence that the terrible scourge had ceased its work of destruction, and departed in search of other and, as yet, unconquered fields. Whatever the anxieties and sympathies of those to whom Barbados is dear may have, in the interim, hoped for us. they will not be disappointed al the continued tale of woe the Steamer bearing this sheet to them carries from our shores. The plague is still amongst us ; virulent þÿ deadly as ever. The most we can sa v is þÿ that it has shifted quarter, and, it may be, that, from causes apart from anything peculiar to the disease itself, its desolation is not now in exactly the same numerical ratio; but the positive affliction it continues to deal out is precisely as it was al the beginning. In other words, þÿ it is steadily retreating from Bridgetown; but like an enemy retreating in good order, and as a matter of choice rather than of necessity, we nevertheless almost daily hear ot some choice victims who have swelled the thousands of its slain. " Whose turn þÿnext? is the interrogatory which every man daily asks himself and his neighbour, and which more aptlv describes ihe position of every class ot the Citizens ol Bridgetown than we could

otherwise describe it, were we to set about to write a column to that end. When we last addressed oui distant triends on this sub ject, guided by the best data that we could get, we estimated me deaths in this parish alone at some 5000 ; since then the number lias been increased by more than 500 þÿ so that we may put down the total at nearly 6000; þÿ fully one seventh of the population þÿ thus exhibiting a picture ot desolation, unprecedented, wc undertake to assert, in the history of this disease during the half century that the civilized world has been acquainted with its tearful history. But what shall we say of the country parishes? We regret to observe that it is next to impossible to procure full particulars of the exact state of things in those distiicts, but accounis, such as they aie, lepresent their condition as positively frightlul From Christ Church. St þÿPhilip s, St. John's, St. James, St. þÿPeter s and other paiishes we hear of little else than the ravages of the destroyer. As an industrious contemporary expresses it neither hill nor dale has been spared. It has raged on the lop of Bissex Hill, and desolated the peaceful plains ol Champaigne ground and Tie Corner 1 he heights ol St. Thomas's and the usually salu brious heights of the picturesque Si John's have been contributing their full quota to the tale ol woe. In the Below Cliff district of the latter, the disease has been tor some time very fatal, laying low ten, eleven and twelve per dav : and we now hear of ii at many

points on the Cliff VVe understand that at Hotliersat's Esiaie the mortality lias been greatest. In the Society's Estates and its neighbourhood, it has declared itsell with so ol much virulence that the Acting Principal tiie College has very judiciously dispersed ihe School for the present, and permitted Ihe Students at the College to icturn to their þÿ homes to do the work of Trinity The calamity ,has been considerably aggravated by the paucity of medical gentlemen in most places In one district of near ten miles, there is but one medical practitioner, and he, we grieve to learn, has been laid aside by a severo attack of the Epidemic. In another extensive parish, we were informed yesterday, there is but one available doctor ; and this, we apprehend is no isolated case. In this emergency, we hear on all sides of the unwearied exertions of the Proprietors and Managers, who obtain the best remedies with which they can make themselves acquainted, are to be found amongsl their labourersday and night, administering medicine and doing all in their power to relieve their necessities."' Much has already been said in favor of Immigration of laborers to this Island ; but a trial, and that may be a dear one, will prove, whether this measure will be beneficial or not. We fear, however, that it will not prove as prosperous as it is anticipated. The Labor Act fixes one uniform pay for first class labourers, (field labourers) and no regard is paid to the amount ot labour which one of these may be able to perform more than another þÿ hence there is no competition ; and the re-

for no labourer will strive to give more work than his fellow labourer, when he knows he cannot receive more wages. If the Labor Act allowed task work and the labourer received wages accordingly þÿ of his hire'7 there is every probability þÿ þÿ the hireling is worthy that some or nearly all of the labourers would do more work than they at present are doing. this, Immigration ma, not be the desideratum j þÿ task work may be more advantageous, it is, however, quite clear, that of the two þÿ tho latter, if tried, would be less expensive.

A þÿ Bill" representing the peculiar condition ol the officers attached to the Garrison in the Danish West India Islands, and recommending an equitable course towards the few who will be found in office at the time of the reduction of the Military Establishment. 2nd Session. 6th Sitting. þÿ1 heooniingency of a reduction of the Military forces in these Islands, within a short period appears inevitable, considering the fact represented by the Government in the statement announcing the increasing deficit during three years, which exhibit a loss to the Treasury þÿ namely : Statement of the Revenue and Disbursements of tho Colony for the year 1850- 1853 inclusive which shows a deficiency of 9 170 841 88 or an average of 35 947 29 The Revenues of the Danish West India Possessions in the financial year 1850-51 amounted to Rbd 325.300 45 and the expenses 624 326 56 Kbd 99.026 I 1 For the Financial vear 1851-52 $ 19,513 06 Revenue Rbd. 562,722 17$ Expenses 595 577 77$ 32.855 60 S 16,427 82 For the Financial year 1852-53 Revenues Rbd. 470.655 62 Expenses 554,460 60 83 801 98 41,901 The deficiencies for the last three years arc 107,841 88 or average amount of 8 35,947 29 The importance of this statement is enhanced by the exigencies of new þÿlaws the prospects for the future in regard of I he Co-

lonial amelioration, subject to the present system, does not offer the probability of averting the continuation of a deficiency of the annual receipts, In such a dilemma, there is no guarantee that the evil will not extend beyond the precedents. Sufficiently serious seenisa result which justifies the anticipation of a change, the ulterior reduction of the Military I1. stab lishment the only alternative to restore the equality of the receipts with the disbursements , and moreover, the means of obtaining a suiplus for local exigencies of an imperative character, that cannot be overlooked. The enactments of laws, increasing the taxation of the Inhabitants, will in their operation hasten the contingency enibiaced in this Bill, inasmuch, that additional burthens on the public aie not based on principles of economy. Measures of this kind belmy the defects þÿ crisis that crisis will be exemplified in ihe of legislation and generally bring on a sudden retrenchments, although beneficial at all times, tiie more so when adopted at an early period. Circumstances may be adduced, as well as prudential considerations which have retarded the reduction of the Military forces in these Islands, and the consequent burthen to the annual Budget. Without presuming to discuss the meriis or imporiance of these allegations þÿ the motives have disappeared and the public mind contemplate the prospective accomplishment of the Act þÿ as an economical project þÿ and the basis of financial im-

provement in the Colonies. The reduction of the Military forces, owing to sound principles of economy, will naturally cause such changes ns will prohnhlv lead lo the withdrawal of some of the officers. The attention of the Council is solicited to the fact, that the pay of these officers exhibits a striking contrast with those of the civil functionaries, as it is shown in the following sketch. Lieutenant Colonel Gicllerup officer in Ihe army from 1819 82400 Major Castonier ditto ditto 1823 1600 Capt. Meincke 1827 a 1300 Holstein 1 832 950 Raupack 1832 950 1st Lieut. Count Knuth 1 834 a 800 H nr hoe 1836 a 800 " Kleist 1837 a 800 Castonier 1838 a 650 þÿ Rosenkraniz 1839 a 650 þÿ Bugel 1841 a 450 þÿ Lnsven 1842 450 The State has by the law of the 5th January 1851, in as far as the mother country is concerned, established fixed rules for the pensioning of Us officials and theri bereaved families for the future. The functionaries in office in the Colonies aie yet deprived of this provision, although the pernicious effects of a debilitating climate render still more gloomv, the prospects of their situation or what it may he when overburthened with broken constitution, or when removed by death from their families. If candour demands the acknowledgment, that the government has olten shown its liberality, in special cases, similar lo such as these remarks are applied in regiuij to ihe Colonies, there yet lemains among the nlficials appointed to this station a natural, and reasonable desire, as well ns anxiety to see

their future position in. this respect also secured by law. Consequently, the object ol this Bill recommends That the Colonial Council requests from the Government the sketch of such a law to he placed before the Council as soon as possible. and in support of this recommendation takes the liberty of drawing the attention ton circumstance which establishes the justice of the case, namely: þÿ That Denmark, in accordance with the examples of the nations possessing Colonies, in stipulating the amount of salary to be retained ns pension, should at the same time, take into consideration the enervating effect »of the climate, and the many privations under which the functionaries labour, therefore, Ihe stipulation of fewer years of previous service than is exncted in the mother country; recommending also, that the pension should be paid, in the same

8 amount of money, whether the pensioner takes up his residence m the Colonies or in Denmark; for if it is alledged by this method, fie may enjoy a somewhat higher pension than that winch is allowed to officers at home, on a par as to rank. It is also natural and just to remaik, that weakened and debilitated from the sad effects of a long residence in a tropical climate, the individual on bein'; compelled to remove to a winter climate will require as absolute necessaries, many things however expensive which another, who has not been so exposed may do without. Moreover, iheamouui whichhe State might in this way economise of the small number of West India pensioners, would not be of much importance, and could not be urged by the State, as it must be a matter of choice with the parties concerned, whether they will remain in the Colonies or remove to take tbeir residence þÿin the mother country. The latter course, considering the reduction of pay, which takes place in cases of such a change, connected with the expenses of the homeward voyage, is often rendered impossible, in cases where it is not only desirable but positively required. It is also worthy of remaik. that the State does not apply this principle to the officials at home who receive the same amount of pension, whether they lake up their residence in the most expensive or cheapest part of the country, although the dtflerence in the price of the necessaries of life, can be the only motive for the difference in the amount of pension.

In conclusion, the Colonial Council takes the liberty to recommend, that in the framing of this law, a proper regard should be had to the condition of the few remaining officers of the former West India Troop, who have served out here under very unfavourable circumstances, and all on very small pay in com pa i tson with t lie salary of civil officials of i tie same standing. It is not necessary, whilst recommending a measure of an equitable character towards the members of a profession worthy of the consideration of the Council, to linger on the higli character and moral principles, which have been maintained, and is generally acknowledged to be due to the officeis of the 1 faulsh armv, lor their exemplary deportment, whilst on the West India station. From the Weekly Record, Grenada, June 29, 1 854. ST. KITTS. It was our inlention to make a few remarks to-day on the annexed extract, kindly forwarded to us by His Excellency ihe Governor. His Excellency has such an abiding interest in every thing that concerns ihe welfare of the Colony, and the importance of the subject is so great, that we regret being obliged to postpone its consideration: þÿ The black and coloured population of the West India Colonies almost universally cultivate the Plantain and Banana trees, for the sake of the fruit; and hitherto, both on their provision grounds and on the plantations, the trees of which the fruit grows have been left in the field to rot. And yet, the fibre of these trees is capable of being converted into Lace, Catnbiics, Shirtings, Sheetings, Ticks, þÿ'l otocls. Cordage, Twines, and Paper ! all of which are in daily use in our families. By far the largest part of the articles thus consumed is now the produce of Slave-labour, and it is the profit which arises from their

owner to buy, work, and sell Slaves Take away the demand of English Ladies for this produce, and one inducement to perpetuate slavery will cease. They cannot compel the American, or the Spanish, or the

Brazilian governments to free their slaves, nor the women of those, and other countries to discourage slavery, but they may discountenance it themselves. Let them try to convert this now wasted material into the means of striking a blow at the accursed system of slavery, and of raising the emancipated Negroes of our Colonies into the condition wc desire, by means of an education which shall be the' reward of their own industry. þÿ Let it be a condition of education in all your schools, that the father, mother, or guardian, of each scholar shall bring to the schoolmaster, or mistress, (every Monday morning, a Plantain or Banana Tree. This will cost him nothing, but the labour ol carrying it from his own ground or from a plantation in which he has only to ask for, in order to obtain it All that is requisite to be done in the school, is to sepernte thp layers, dry them in the sun, pack them in bundles, and deliver them to a carrier to be conveyed to a receiver in the nearest shipping port Certainly ha þÿIf an-hour in the morning, to carry out. and hang upon lines, ihe layers to dry. and to take them in at night, will be all ihe labour required from ihe children ; the master or mistress tying them up in bundles at the end of every week, and delivering them to the carrier. The merchant who is the shipping agent in the town will have them packed as close as possible, and they may then be forwarded to England. A person appointed for the purpose will receive them in London or

Liverpool, where they may be very easily ami The Price of the Shares is as follows: þÿ cheaply prepared for Ihe use ol the manufacturers, bv whom they will be made up into such articles as are in daily consumption in each of your families. You will have only to resort to the shop in which these articles are sold, to purchase them at their market value, and to use them in preference to articles made by slave labour So much for our part of the business. Now let us see what will he the eftiect in the West Indies, and on the funds of the Society. þÿ In 1 lie West Indies, the scholars will fie taught that their own industry has contributed to secure to them the blessings of a truly useful and religious education ; that industry is no longer a badge ol slavery, but a most honorable means of obtaining the highest enjoyment, and the most true and perminent blessings. The scholars, the parents, and the teachers will all feel sympathy with you, and vou will become fellmv workers with Him who declares that both He and His Father are ever at work lor the regeneration and happiness of mankind. þÿ Now, as to the effect on your funds. Your last report shows, that there are þÿ in ihe schools patronized and sustained by you, 5702 pupils Every Plantain or Banana Tree will produce 4lbs fibre, and if we calculate this at only Id per lb. in the unmanufactured state, the raw material will oive to your funds the enormous sunt of £4857 10s. per annum, nearly five times the amount ol your annual þÿsubscriptions. To the Editor of the St. Croix Aids. Dear Sir, Although the published accounts of the matters discussed in the Colonial Council are miserably meagre, and convey but a very, sparing notion to the public of what takes place in that body; yet I am happy to say, there are members of that assembly, who do think that the people of this Island have an interest in the proceedings which take place there and sometimes give their friends an idea of what so much concerns them. In this wav, 1 understand, that great exception was taken in the Council to-day in regard to the remarks which you made in the Avis of the 25th inst. , in connexion with the new Lira ( t of Law introduced, relative to the importation of foreign Labourers. Indeed the article was considered of sufficient importance, and withal of so mischievous a tendency, as to call forth especial refulation ; and the astonishment of one honorable member was even expressed, that such an article was permitted to find its way into the public press. This strange remark coming from a member of what I believe is generally considered in this Island a popular Assembly, I shall pass over without comment, but 1 reallv cannot see what evil there could be apprehended from your expressing your opinion on the subject ; albeit that may not be a very sanguine one. I am myself a strong advocate for the importation of foreign laborers, and fully believe it to be a measure highly necessary for the welfare of this Colony ; but 1 do not think that Flamers should feel so easilv star-

If any one of them considers that he has used all proper, persevering, and judicious means to encourage and promote task- work on his Estate, by which it is well known, by all experience in the English Islands, cheaper and more extensive work can be obtained : if he feels satisfied on this point, then let him ask þÿhimself how many able men he has withdrawn from the so called þÿ field þÿwork, and employed as cartmeu, ploughmen, and to drive weeding machines, &c., under the express stipulation that they should not be reaequired, is to he ihe male teacher. quired to work with the hoe or cut canes I would not hint, of course, that any one of them would take his þÿneighbor s people who j were in the habit of working in the field and employ them for such purposes. Oh, no I would not do this (for 1 am sure there me some who would not do so.) 15m 1 would say that if there is one whose conscience can acquit him of proceedings so inimical to his own and tlic general interest, then I think that he not only has a right to feel indignant, but he can justly consider himself a rare ex ccption amongst his brethren. This perm cious practice, let me seriously rcmaik, is, I fear, too universal throughout the Island. þÿ Every estate has more or less people engaged under these especial provisions ; but the svs tem has been carried out to such an extent

by some, that if equally adopted by all, it may be inferred that ere long none but wo men will be left to perform the field work. The second Session of the Colonial Council is now about to close, and it is too late perhaps to bring forward any new measure; but it is to be regretted that the session should be closed without a clause having been added to the Labor Act, which would depiivo Planters of the power of injuring themselves by persisting in the system alluded to. By the FJarl Dnndonald we received a letter from a friend in New Y"ork. dated the 31st ulto.. containing the following : þÿ þÿ Mr. Cunard has just published a notice to the effect " that the Steam Communication between this Port, Bermuda and the West Indies is discontinued from this date." þÿ Nothing can exceed the indignation of all parties interested in this City, at this proceeding, and you in Bermuda, 1 know, will share this feeling. The ostensible reason for the discontinuance of the line is that it was not paying its expenses. However good a reason this may be it cannot be considered justifiable in the absence of timely notice to the public. The inconvenience occurring to mercantile interests and to the travelling public on this route, cannot be estimated 1 hope however, it may lead to a more efficient line being established by some of our energetic American þÿCompanies. þÿ Ibid.

The þÿ Curlew. Tiie non-arrival of the Cunard screwsteamer Curlew, Captain Sampson, on the 17th of last month, we nvoided to remark on, in the absence of reliable information, al though wc previously knew it was unlikely that she was coming, and that the route of New York, Bermuda, and St. Thomas, bad been changed on the grounds of a statement we made in the Tidbnde, ol the 28th May, 1853, viz , that the line was not lemuncrnt ing, but the contrary, a loss to the projectors. At that time, however, the British Admiralty found it inconvenient to suspend the line in consequence of remonstrances made, and was accordingly allowed to linger on one year longer. Many at the same time regretting that it was permitted to live on so long at the expense of their sailing vessels, which would have had the passenger and freight business in the event of a steamer failing to do the work. The injuiy done to the public in the West indies and the United States by the suspension of a regular mail conveyance and certainly of travelling must be mallets clear to every individual at all conversant will) the benefits devolving on commerce where tegular and certain communication and intercourse can be kept up. The withdrawal of the Steamer from New York will inflict without doubt an injury to the general interests of commerce here, and once more place in the hands of a few that participation in business which should belong to all, and on this score we must re-iterate the hope the Bermudians have expressed that a line may

yet be established by some enterprising company in the Union. By the arrival ol the Curlew, on Saturday last, from Halifax and Bermuda, and the opportunity of a short conversation with Uaptain Sampson, wc are enabled in the absence of any printed report to state what are the changes regarding the future arrival of that vessel here. The point of departure of the Curlew will hereafter be Halifax, calling at Bermuda, and proceeding to St. Thomas, and back bv the same route.

The departure will he once in every four weeks, and so arranged that she will carry the Outward European Mail to Bermuda from Liverpool via Halifax to Boston; and receive the American Mail destined for the West Indies by the Boston steamer bound to Europe via Halifax. The Curlew will always await the arrival of the outward and homeward bound steamers, and will start from Halifax two hours after the arrival ol the last. By this means we shall still pos sess a steam communication with the United Slates and British North America, only more circuitous, delaying, and expensive. An American booking-office we are told will be started at Halifax, which will afford passen gers from the West Indies in the Curlew through Tickets to New York for $12 þÿ to avoid proceeding in the Boston steamer, which alone would cost $ 20. A passenger receiving a Ticket from the above office will be conveyed by stage to Winslow town, 40 miles from Halifax, across the Bay of Fundy by steam to Portland, and thence by train to New York. This no doubt will become the preferable load Passengers and mails Irom St. Thomas will arrive in New York in ten days after the day of starting, The line ol country to be passed over we should also think would be very desirable to travellers.

Novel Surgical Operation A most singular and successful operation was performed in Pittsburgh a few days since. John Greener, a lad about ten years of age, residing lin the Filth Ward of that City, was playing with a fish honk, by holding it in Ins mouth, when, by some mishap, he swallowed it. He tried to remove it by pulling at the string, hut it had become iirntly lodged in the lower and hack part of the throat. The little fellow was not only frightened but in great pain ; attempts were made by the þÿhoy s parents to extract the hook, hut they were unable to do it. The hook had become firmly imbedded in the throat. Hr. A. Walters was called, and after many fruitless efforts he at length hit upon this novel and ingenious plan to extract it. Having ascertained the pro liable size of the hook, ,a pistol-bullet ot suitable dimensions was procured, a hole was pierced in the middle of it, and placed upon the line of the fishhook, and allowed to slip down to the hook, The weight of the bullet, assisted by gentle pressure downwards with a pair of curved forceps, removed the hook from its situation. Thus liberated, the point ofthe hook sticking into the lend, and being protected by it, was safely removed.

Front the St. Thomas Times, August 5. The British Virgin Islniids.

Our advices from Tortola state that the new President, Mr. Kortright, had arrived at Road Town, and was already making himself very popular among the people. The two branches of the Legislature were, however, at variance, owing to some important measures which had passed the Lower House having been rejected by the Upper House, without even a Conference. Among the Bills ' passed by the Assembly, we are told, was one doing away entirely with the present Constitution of the British Virgin Islands, and substituting a new one in lieu ; it was also proposed to abolish the Representative Assembly and to have in place a Legislative Council. Another of the Bills was one repealing all former Bills tending to taxation, duties, &c., ; and establishing an uniform rate of 2A per cent on the value of every article of export or home consumption ; this scale extended to house assessments, boat licences, cattle tax, &,c. Owing to the refusal on the part of the Council to entertain either of these Bills the House of Assembly came to the determination to suspend all further business, pending a dissolution by the Executive. A few of the troops were still at Tortola.

The following from the Panama Star ami Ilcrnltl, may throw some light on the recent piratical destruction of Greytown, and account for the American Cortimander addressing his proclamation to the " pretended authorities" of that place though it does not justify the outrage : þÿ " Nicaragua. þÿ By the arrival of the steamer Daniel Webster at New Orleans, from 8an Juan, the papers of that city have the following news from Nicaragua : " On the 18th, the day following the departure of the Northern Light, the British war steamer Argus arrived from Bolivia, en route for Jamaica. The people of San Juan del Norte, applied ! to the commander for protection, and for an order to disperse the force of fifty men under command of Major Fletcher, left by Mr. Borland, the U. S. Minister, for the protection of the property and interests of the Transit Company at I'unta the Arenas. 'This was not granted, and the steamer sailed on the 21st nil. On the same day the Mayor of San Juan notified the United Slates Consul Mr. Fabins, of his resignation and total dissolution of the city. The place is now without any form of government or law. The station, arms and ammunition are now in possession of Jamaica negroes þÿ the same party who committed the unparalleled outrage upon the person of the American Minister. The wise provision of Mr. Borland in leaving an armed force for the protection of the Accessory Transit Company has probably prevented the repetition of outrages more serious than any which

have heretofore occurred. In the interior of Nicaragua things are in the same unsettled condition. The revolutionary party, under Mnnoz and Castillon, having defeated Chimono at Chenandagua, LtAin, Manigua, Masaya, have now marched upon Granada, where Chimono and his party are prepared for a formidable resistant e. It is safe to

predict that the revolutionary party will prevail and the new government will be in possession of affairs before the departure of the next steamer. We learn from Mr. Beard, a passenger direct from Granada, that the revolutionary party have assailed Granada and had carried the place. þÿ They had defeated the government troops in everv part of the town. The houses were ini mediately forced and consumed in which the government party took refuge. Great confusion prevailed. Our informant was shot at eleven times while endeavoring 1o get to the beach of Lake Nicaragua in order to decamp.' "

Special Dispatch to the N. Y. Tribune. Washington, Friday, June 30, 1854. Important and highly interesting intelligence from Madrid anil Faris has reached the Depart me n I ofSiaie. In spile of all his efforts and all his diplomatic seductions, Mi. Soule has not succeeded either in restoring an entente cordiale with Spain or in doing anything toward the purchase of Cuba, the Queen of the Antilles The obstinacy which the Spanish Government manifests in the settlement of the Cuban difficulty, is to he attributed to two causes. First. They are confident of the support nl Fiance and England in case of emcrgenev. Second. They do not believe the United Slates Government is in earnest No treaty has yet been concluded between France, England and Spain on this subject ; but the preliminary steps for such a treaty were made some time ago, and only failed til consummation because England gave notice that she should insist upon the insertion of a clause in regard to slavery in Cuba which was so obnoxious to the Spanish Government, that the negotiation was suspended. Since then Spain has offered France ten thousand men to supply the place of the ten thousand French soldiers in Rome, to permit the latter to join the ninrv in Turkey, on condition that she will pledge her suppoit against the United States in case of a war Louis Napoleon refused the ptoposilion, hecause alone, he could not enter into a wai with the United States. Besides, a war between these two ancient allies would he as

repugnant to the Government and people ol France as to those of the United States The feeling ol friendship lor our nation is so strong in France that il might become a question whether, if Louis Napoleon was disposed to push his people into a war with us, it would not cost him his throne. For a purely national and palpable cause it is possible that the French people could he brought into a state of mind hostile to the people of the United States ; hut for a war in which they felt no direct interest, and into which they should be forced merely to accomplish n bargain, it may be salelv predicted they would not engage However this may be, it is well known that the Spanish Government counts largely on the aid of France, and her hopes lie principally in the influence which the Empress is supposed to exert on the destinies of the country. In a recent number of the Tribune the rase of Mr Menard was mentioned, an American citizen who had been claimed by the French Government, subjected to the conscription, and drawn as n recruit into the French army. The history of the case I am now enabled to state more in detail than was done in the

Tribune's paragraph; it is briefly as follows: þÿ The father of Mr. Menard is a French citizen who lived twenty-five years in the United States without being naturalized. While there he married an American woman by whom he had sevetal children, one of whom is the young man in question. Some time ago, and after an absence of twenty-five years in the United States, as just stated, Mr. Menard, Senr., with his entire family, returned to Bordeaux in France, his former residence, and settled. His family, as it will be observed, entirely of American origin, entered France by means of American passports, while the father, having preserved his nationality, entered by means of a French passport, The French Government now claims the children of Mr. Menard as French citizens, and has accordingly subjected the son to the conscription. It does this upon the local law of France, which makes parentage the title of nationality. On this ground the French Cabinet manifests a determination to persist in its claims on this man, in opposition to the reclamations which our Legation has made in his behalf. These reclamations, it appears, have been based principally upon the following facts : þÿ 1. The general law of nations, in opposition to the local law of France, recognizes soil as the title of nationality. 2. The mother of young Menard was an American born citizen. 3. The French Government had indirectly admitted bis American nationality by permitting him to land upon French territory with an American passport. They bad fur-

ther admitted it by the following circumstance i A cousin of young Menard, born on American soil, like himself, with one parent American, and having entered France in the same way. wishing to get married, was compelled, as an American citizen, to have the civil part of the ceremony performed by the American Consul at Bordeaux. It is not ascertained whether young Menard left the United States before attaining the age which would have entitled him to the exercise of his rights as an American citizen or not. But this circumstance cannot seriously invalidate the justice of the claim which the Government of the United States makes in his behalf However, it is expected that t tic French Government, recognizing only as its guide the local law of France, will decide against the application for his liberation, in which case the family, being rich, will buy a substitute under protest. The affair will then be referred to Washington for settlement. In the mean lime Menard has been allowed his liberty until a decision can be had. <> <«

I'rom the Son Fernando Gazelle. " We have been favoured with a sight of a letter from Dr. Gavin, in which he almost prophetically warns West Indians that they must expect Cholera throughout their Islands this year. We are not alarmists, and believe that a bountiful Providence has endowed this Island with a finer climate than most of our neighbours enjoy ; still there is ampleoccasion for us to he on our guard. It is absolutely necessary that our dwellings and their environs should be purged from filth : that in crowded neighbourhoods and crowded houses lime washing should be had recourse to, and that lime should be unsparingly used to neutralize the evil effects of substances which give out fetid odors, Without this be done there can he no safety. All persons should be very careful in their diet, and particularly so as regards water for drinking. " It is to be particularly observed that, before an attack of Cholera, there is always a looseness of the bowels, which Medical men therefore call a premonitory symptom ; that this state, after continuing a short time, during which the patient

8 IT, Ui I ATI 8, feels no uneasiness, passes suddenly into the fatal stage, if Medical aid is had recourse to nine persons outof ten recover; hut if they wait for the second stage, before calling in the Doctor in nine cases of ten they have lost their chance of recovery. " We therefore recommend our neighbours to be on their guard, and, if they perceive any premonitory symptom, to go immediately to the Doctor ; and we hope the Doctors will encourage them to do so by dispensing a remedy in such cases at as low a charge as will remunerate them for their trouble. " We say nothingat present respecting the duty of Town Councils and Boards of Health, because we do not think that any extraordinary exertions on their part are required until we hear that the disease is nearer to us ; hut we trust they will hold themselves ready to act in the most strenuous manner if necessity should arise. In the mean time we will hope that, as heretofore, the destroyer will pass our highly favoured Island."

The West Indian furnishes us with an article on the subject of cholera, from the pen of ihe celebrated English Chemist, Mr. Herapath, ol Bristol We recommend its careful perusal, and although it was written in November 1847, yet it is applicable to any period. The writer says: þÿ " We regret that there is every probability of this fearful scourge again appearing among us. It is now in Russia, making fearful havoc, and progressing westward in the same way it did fifteen years since Mr. Hernpath, a chemist of Bristol, who during the last visitation of the cholera in this country made the disease the subject of minute and elaborate observations and experiments, has written a letter to the Times from which we subjoin an extract. Mr. Herapath states as the result of his researches : þÿ 1. That the cause of cholera is a putrid animal poison, capable of being recognised by the smell by some, emanating from and surrounding the dead or living cholera subject or articles of clothing þÿ 2. That it is not sulphuretted hydrogen or hydrosulphurct ol ammonia, as it does not decompose salts of lead or zinc, and when passed through nitrate of silver it only forms a red solution when exposed to liyht þÿ 3. That it is only received into the living body through the lungs, and cannot be propagated by innoculation. þÿ 4. That infection can be conveyed by articles ol clothing, bedding, etc. : and that washerwomen are mote subject to infection than ordinary persons from that cause þÿ 5. That all

persons are not equally liable to infection from equal exposure, and even the same individual becomes more sensitive under certain circumstances þÿ 6. That the poison is destroyed by chloride gas and a heat of 300 deg, Fahrenheit. "' The two most powerful disinfectants of the day þÿ the chloride of zinc and the nitrate of lead, known as Sir W. Barnel's and Ledoyen's þÿ will be of no avail, although they will promptly remove ordinary putrid effluvia. The only chemical preventive I depended upon in my numerous exposures to the virus was chloiine gas, and this I believe to be a perfect one if the fumigation is complete. I invariably passed through an atmosphere of it on my return home, and kept it escaping through my residence during the continuance of the disease in the city. I also placed large quantities of she substance necessary for the evolution of this gas in the hands of the Bristol druggist, who was kind enough to distribute 1,200 quantities of it gratuitously to applicants during three days with instructions for the use, and am happy to say that duiing that time the deaths fell from ton to one per day, and I have but little doubt that if every ship arriving in England from an infected place should be exposed to a perfect fumigation with chlorine, we shall be preserved from the infection. If the disease should pass this cordon, by any accident, then every house in the infected district should be stmultaneoiislv

fumigated with it þÿ say three limes a day : unless done in all houses at the same lime it would be useless, or nearly so ; and to do i! effectually, a mixture of three parts ol common salt and one of black oxide of manganese should be placed just inside the outer or street door of the dwelling-house, and a little common vitrol poured upon it. The inward current of air will convey the chlorine gas to every part of the interior, and wherever it can be smelt the effect is produced þÿ the miasm is destroyed. If articles ol clothing are infected, and the colours likely to be injured by the gas, they may be heated in an oven or on a kiln, to 250 or 300 degrees (about the heat of baking bread), when they might be " þÿ punity.' Watch it night and day for a week, and you will never sec it. growing ; but return after two months, and you will find it all whitening for the harvest. Who are the Truly Valuable in Society. þÿ The value set upon a member of society, should be not according to the fineness or intensity of his feelings, to the acuteness of his sensibility, or Ins readiness to weep for, or deplore the misery lie may meet in the world ; but in proportion to the sacrifices which he is ready to make, and to the knowledge and talents which he is able and willing to contribute towards removing the misery. To benefit mankind is a much more difficult task than some seem to imagine ; it is not quite so easy as to make a display of amiable sensibility ; the first requires long study and painful abstinence front the various alluring pleasures by which we are surrounded ; the second in most cases demands only a little acting, and even when sincere is utterly useless to the public. þÿ IVeslmin Her Review.

Women and Ladies. þÿ In the days of our fathers there were such beings to be met with as men and women ; hut now they are all gone, and in their place a race of gentlemen and ladies þÿ be still more refined, a race of " ladies or, to and gentlemen" þÿ has sprung up. Women and girls arc among the things that were; but "ladies" are found elsewhere. Miss Martineau, wishing to see the wowas answered by the warden. " We men wards in a prison in Tennessee, have no ladies here at present, madam." Now so far as the ladies were concerned, it was very well that none of them were in prison ; but then it sounds a little odd þÿ ladies in prison ! It would seem had enough for women to be in such a place. A lecturer, discoursing upon the characteristic of women, illustrated thus : þÿ Who were the last at the cross? Ladies. Who were the lirstat the sepulchre? Ladies. On the modern improvement we have heard hut of one thing that heats the above. It was the finishing touch to a marriage ceremony, performed by an exquisite divine up to all modern refinements. When lie had thrown the chain of Hymen round the happy couple, he concluded by saying þÿ " I now pronounce you husband and lady." The audience stuffed their handkerchiefs into their mouths and got outof the room as quickly as possible to take their breath þÿ Washington (N. ('.) font.

The period, which is grunted to laborers in the country, to give notice to remove from one estate to another on the 1st of October, having now arrived, we beg to offer a few remarks on the subject of removal among the rural population. It has been said, the truth ot which we cannot vouch for, that some of the planters, during the last period of removal, enticed laborers to their estates, by bribery and false promises, and not a few succeeded in this illegal method to obtain a large number of laborers ; but this system is very pernicious both to the planter and the laborer ; for in nine cases out of ten the laborer is dissatisfied and the planter deceived þÿ the laborer soon after feelsadisconteuted and regrets leaving the former estate, which perhaps lie abandoned from some trivial cause, and the planter, finding that the laborer performs his work with indifference, resorts to measures which very often prove unsatisfactory to both parties. If fair and legal means of employing laborers were adopted by all the planters, things would work better, and the authorities would, doubtless, be spared all that trouble they experience in settling differences between laborers and their employers. We cannot think of a better and safer method of bringing the country people to understand the evil of unnecessary removal, than through the different ministers, who, we are sure, will agree with us and say, that more than two thirds or nearly all of the people who remove, soon find out that they

In giving our opinion on the draft of a law relating to Commerce and Shipping in St. Thomas, we beg leave to offer the following remarks : We fully agree with regard to the necessity pointed out by the Government, that of regulating the Customhouse relations in St. Thomas by a new law. AV ith regard to the duties on Goods, then in case the draft be made into law, there will not be introduced any other essential alterations in what actually exists, than that some Colonial Goods, which pass through St. Thomas, which have hitherto been assessed at a higher rate than other Goods, will according to 4 I and 13 of the draft be placed on an equal footing with other goods, which we cannot but approve of, notwithstanding the State Treasury thereby will have to give up an annual revenue of about $1500. The tonnage dues however tend to a more extensive alteration of the existiug rules, that of | placing all vessels of the same burthen on an equal tooting, and thus do away with the distinction existing in regard of European vessels, in contra distinction to vessels belonging to places situated to the West of the Atlantic, which dis- j linction, in conformity with those documents to which we have had access, has not been exercised þÿ'' Tore the year 1819 in consoquence of Admiralty dues. This point of the ease has been the

® ut ® a x &'ns, subject of the most particular deliberations, and as there seems to exist no real cause to introduce this distinction, the Council, in referring to the freight charges consider it in complete accordance with equity, that this distinction be done away with now, as it is in contemplation to regulate the Custom-house relations by a new law, which must be considered the more desirable, as by these means an opportunity will offer, as proposed in the draft, to confer a boon on Navigation, viz : that the tonnage-dues be regulated according to the quantity of the goods discharged or laden, which was not provided for by the older provisions, and the want of which has been sadly felt. In proceeding to the special provisions of the draft, and in as far as we think that any alterations ought to be proposed, we beg leave to state : ad 2 I. A. From the St. Thomas Times, August 16. j THE þÿ CONWAY. Tnr. K. M þÿCompany steam-ship s Conway Captain Powell, arrived here at midnight on Monday from Windward, and anchored ofl the port. It was ascertained very early next morning that five cases of Cholera were on board among the crew, supposed to have been taken at Grenada, the Conway having coaled alongside the Company's wharf at that Island, i She has been strictly denied by our Authorities all pratique with the shore, and the passengers þÿ ten for Europe, four for St. Thomas, and two for America þÿ still continue on board. Remonstrances have bpen made by the passengers of the Alrato, the Ship for Southampton, and last from Jamaica, to receive the Conway's passengers on boaid the former vessel, and we learn the temonstrance emanates chiefly from Jamaica passengers This reminds us of the story of the Pot and the Kettle. Passengers (rom Jamaica þÿ a place now invariably infected with Cholera to þÿ refuse to meet with passengers from the vicinity of a like infected place, seems odd to us. But the Captains and Doctors will decide otherwise. The mails from the Conway were not landed here till a late hour yesterday þÿafternoon having previously undergone a powerful fumigntion. One case of Cholera up to last night terminated fatally on board, and the accounts to that time say that the remaining four indicate symptoms of recovery. The steamer was at sea all last night, and is about mid-channel this morning The evil now to be dealt with is. how is the Con-

way to fie coaled T Where is our quarantine ground and safe place of anchorage beyond the harbour for vessels with diseases on board? Where are our Lazarettos todivide the healthy from the sick ? We ask for an answer to these questions of those who love our Island so well þÿ who have labored for it so long and so effectually, without pay and without emolument ! One fearful theme alone pervades the minds of the inhabitants of the Islands to Windward and the writers of newspapers, participating in the general gloom, occupy their sheets, to the almost entire exclusion of other subjects, in dissertations on CHOLERA I In nearly every paper wc find a mournful catalogue, indicating that the ctuel destroyer continues his deadly work At Barbados the pestilence has swept off over eighteen thousand souls þÿ among these 326 military. The Globe, of the 10th remarks þÿ þÿ It is a great misfortune certainly to be unable to commence our present brief summary of local events, for the special information of distant friends and readers, without the gratifying announcement that the dread þÿVisitor itas wholly and finnally taken its departure It yet lingers amongst us ; but, whilst it occasionally makes its presence felt very keenly by the occurrence in Town and Country of some case of marked malignity, there is vet every evidence of indisposition further to propagate itself, and its gradual disappearance is as decided as its ravages have been frightful." GRENADA has also suffered severely þÿaltho the Epidemic is said to be decidedly

on the decline. A private letter, dated 8ih instant, says: þÿ I am happy to mention that the Cholera has nearly disappeared from the Island at the present time ; there are but a few solitary cases here and there The total number of deaths exceeds 3,000, out of a population of 32 000. This calamity will throw Grenada back for 10 or 15 þÿyears The Chronicle,, Aug. 5, also contains the following paragraph: þÿ We are gratified in being able to pronounce the Epidemic to be greatly on the decline, ns compared with its ravages up to the end of last week ; and should it please the Almighty, in His great mercy, to permit its declination in the same ratio for a week or two more, we may hope to be enabled, in our next .Summary, to report the Colony very nearly, if not altogether, free of the pestilence. The centre of the Russian army is advancing on Kalugereni ; the right wing, under Liprandi, is marching back toward Fokschani, so that their new position is in a convex form, turned towards the Danube, with the wings drawn back. The Ottomans have occupied Giurgevo with 60,000 men, and are constructing most extensive entrenchments.

Omar Pasha was proceeding to Rutschnk with a body of 30,000 men ; 25,000 Ottoman troops, with 5,000 cavalry, are already there Captain llyde Parker, of the Firebrand, was killed by the enemy at the attack on Sulina. Five Greeks attempted to assassinate Lord Raglan on the 2nd of July. The one who fired was hanged, the others flogged. The fleets were at Baltschik on the 10th. The Austrian troops have entered VVallachia. THE BALTIC. The fleet on the 17th was proceeding to Aaland. The cases of cholera had diminished in number since the fleet had left Cronstadt. THE REVOLUTION IN SPAIN. At Madrid, on the 19th, barricades were erected in every part of the city ; and fighting was going on in every quarter. Valladolid pronounced on the 16th; the Captain- General and the Governor are arrested ; Progressista generals command the troops. The Sartorius Ministry has resigned, and the Queen has called General Cordova to her councils. At 10 þÿo clock p. m. on the 17th, a popular rising took place at Madrid ; the populace were armed, and, under the guidance of their leaders, were masters of Madrid all the night, and continued so at one p.m. of the 18th. All Catalonia has risen, and the Captain-General heads the movement. The Basque provinces have also risen. General Espartero and General Zabala arc marching on Saragossa, to place themselves at the head ot the movement. A battle had been fought near Grenada, between þÿO Donnell and General Blazer, in which the latter and
Count Vista Hermosa had been wounded and taken prisoners. þÿ Ibid, July 23.

The "AVIS." Christiansted , Tuesday the 22nd August 1S54. THE ROADS. In our paper of the 4ili instant we adverted to the had condition of the roads in the Western vicinity of this town. We have since heard several persons complaining not only of the had state of these roads, hut also of the like condition of the roads in Rastend. The latter, which have never heen in perfect order, even when attention was paid to them, must now, when so nuvli neglected, he considered almost impassaide. It is very strange to observe how indifferently the planters regard the condition of the roads and what little regard the way-wardens attend to their duties which, it appears, are considered of very little consequence ; hut in reality, are of great importance ; for no one can predict the danger that might accrue either to persons or animals from travelling on bad roads. We hope, however, that these brief remarks will open the eyes of those directly concerned, and something done to remedy the evil we speak of.

HOGS. We fear that the late police regulation regarding dogs does not extend to the country, not to speak of the town nt present ; for if it did the Inspector of the Prison would not he allowed to keep so many, and thus prevent the public from making use of the pleasant roads around the Prison, as these dogs attack indiscriminately every person riding, driving or walking. It is our opinion that if the Inspector is to have ilogs, he must keep them chained, and not a'low them to disturb any person passing the prison, for the roads are public and have been, until very recently, much frequented.

The Berlingske paper of the 25th July contains an article, taken from an English paper, regarding the English vessel that was unintentionally fired into from one of the forts at St. Thomas. The paper states that an English vessel had been fired into with red-hot halls (gloende Kugler) and that indemnity to the amount of $1500 had been given. This is incorrect, and it is quite absurd to suppose that red-hot halls would he used to stop a vessel. The amount of indemnity given was $500 and not $1500 as erroneously stated.

As the ordinance of the 6th September 1S53 makes a distinction between Merchants and Retailers in possession of burgherbrief and sellers by licence, and as it would probably not be light to refuse these petty dealers the assistance by the Custom-house making out their entries, to do which they may be supposed to want the requisite knowledge, we unanimously propose with 15 votes, that the word " Commercial-houses in the place" be altered to "Merchants." Ad i 19 and 29. In as far as the first mentioned paragraph in the 2d section orders, that discharging and loading shall take place front sunrise to sunset, and paragraph 20 contains punishment by the forfeiture of the goods in case anything is discharged or laden beyond the time specified, the Colonial Council must observe, that the circumstance, that vessels in the harbor of St. Thomas cannot load or discbarge goods at the laud itself but when at anchor, sometimes at no shjrt distance from the shore, renders it difficult to determine beforehand the time for completing the work, especially when casual circumstances occur, such as rain or blustering weather sets in Nor has such a limited time been hitherto maintained, in consequence wherefore the packets plying between St. Croix and St. Thomas as well as the Spanish schooners have been able, when pre-

vented from taking in their whole cargo during the course of the day to take off the balance of the cargo, lying at the wharves of the merchants, after sunset, and to sail in the course of the night, having previously obtained a night-pass from the fort. In order to maintain the advantage thus hitherto bestowed on the shipping and at same time to preserve good order with regard to the transportation of merchandise in the harbor, we arc of opinion that this might be obtained by these means, that tho ordinary time be extended to one hour after sunset, and in case any further time be exceptionally desired, that report be previously made to the Customs. From these considerations a majority of 12 votes against 3 agreed to propose : that the words in the 2d section of the 19th paragraph " to sunset" bo superceded by " until one hour after sunset" ; and with 13 votes against 2, that in paragraph 20 after the 2d section be added : " except report be previously made to the Customs." with 15 votes, that "25" in the 5th line be altered to " 10." Ad 23. The Burgher Council has proposed, that the minister of Finances be empowered to grant alleviations with regard to the amount of the tonnage dues and fees to the Harbormaster, for vessels importing only coals for the use of the British Steam Packet Company, and which instead of leaving in ballast take in articles amounting to £ or £ of the burthen of the vessel. In consideration of that said vessels, generally speaking are of great burthen and with special regard to their not having to pay anything when leaving in ballast, and as it would be too oppressive for them to pay the full amount of duties When having a small quantity of articles onboard, the Colonial Council begs leave to recommend, that the minister of Finances be authorized to grant that the tonnage dues and the fees to the Harbormaster for such vessels be reduced to the same amount as if they were entered in ballast. By these means the merchants may have an opportunity of getting goods shipped by the vessels to the place where they are destined in order to take a homeward cargo to Europe, and thus these vessels would yield some revenue to the State Treasury, instead of its getting nothing at all, as it would answer the purpose better to let them quit St. Thomas in ballast, than to pay the full duties for an inconsiderable quantity of goods.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir! Having been credibly informed that you were appointed Agent for the Sale of Tickets in the Great Hessian State Lotteries, and that you are not in possession of the last Official Drawing, I beg leave to state, that I consider it your duty to notify Messrs. A. Schwarz- 8cltild &. Co. of Lombard street, London, that owing to their negligence you have not received the long expected List of Drawn Numbers, and that as a consequence, a great many persons to whom you sold Tickets, avail themselves of every opportunity to evince their dissatisfaction, and give expression to sentiments that are calculated to destroy the celebrity of the Hessian Lotteries, and effectually prevent a sale of the Tickets in this Island I beg leave to add, that in my opinion, the Hessian Lotteries are conducted on principles that are not understood by nine tenths of the purchasers of the Tickets, and I think it necessary that you should inform Messrs. Schwarzchilds that unless they will give you satisfactory elucidations relative to their Lotteries, and be punctual in forwarding the Lists of Drawn Numbers, it would be better to confine the sale of their Tickets to places where they have a better reputation, and larger circulation, as it cannot be reasonably expected that persons here who assert, that they have been imposed on, and neglected, will again be allured by illusory inducements to purchase Tickets from you, or any other person that may offer them for

sale. The Prospectus of the Great Hessian State Lottery which you published in May last, informed the Public that on the 1st of June there would he a drawing of 20 Series consisting of 500 Bond Numbers, which Bond Numbers, by the drawing of the 1st July, would become entitled to 500 Prizes. The Holder of a Drawn Number of the Series had therefore I presume, a reason to suppose that he was entitled to 25 Bond Numbers, and if he was aware that Drawn Numbers of the Series are to be redeemed by Bond Numbers, he had also a right to expect that he would be placed in possession of the Bond Numbers previous to the Drawing that would entitle them to Prizes. If the Holder of a Drawn Number of the Series is entitled to only one instead of Twenty five Bond Numbers, why are the Bond Numbers not circulated instead of the Series ? and if it is necessary that the Scries shall be circulated to be redeemed when drawn, by Bond Numbers, why are the Bond Numbers not sent to their respective destinations previous to the drawing that entitle them to Prizes? If Messrs. J. A. Sclnvarzschild Sons have made the necessary arrangements, that the amount of the Prizes gained in their Lotteries, can be cashed through an established Bank, can you inform me whether their arrangements extend to the Banks established in the Danish West India Colonies? If these are questions that you do not feel yourself qualified to answer, I hope they will be answered by other persons, whose better qualifications ought to enable them to reply in a satis-

factory manner. I cannot refrain from hoping, that the complicated, impenetrable, and mysterious something, that is supposed to be connected with the Hessian Lotteries, exists only in the minds of interested parties, and as I trust you will avail yourself of every opportunity to obtain such information, as will be satisfactory, when imparted to those who purchased Tickets from you, I will be happy to aid in

str» © » ® a st ah exonerating you from unmerited censure. Yours Respectfully, # # St. Croix, August 25th 1854. The remarks made in the above article are just. We agree with the author in saying that there is every reason for dissatisfaction. We received no other list of drawn numbers, but that which appeared in our paper of the 4th July last þÿ a list of 20 numbers. We regret to say that it is not in our power to offer any explanation. We have written to the House for a list of the numbers drawn on the 1st July; but have not been favored with any. Should we be so fortunate as to receive the scheme by the next packet, no time will be lost in bringing it before the public. þÿ Ed

PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session Report to His Majesty. The Colonial Council has been entrusted with the charge to report on the draft of law containing some provisions relative to the taxation on buildingB in tho Danish Woetindia Islands according to the ordinance of 1st October 1802. The Council coincides in the views on which the 1st clause of -the draft of law are based, and are of opinion, that the draft ought to be adopted As this tax however is supposed to bo applicable only with regard to servant's rooms in the towns, it is deemed neoessary that this be expressly stated. The Council is aware of, that building tax of late years has beon assessed on dwellings in the oountry and laborers' houses on estates when rented out. This system of taxation is based on the resolution of the Ministry of Fioanoe dated 24th October 1849, published by the Government Secretary on the 27th November ensuing. The Council think that the tax itself is not unfair, as the said buildings yield an increased revenue to the owners, but as doubt has been expressed, in how far the said resolution is warranted by the ordinance of the 1st October 1802, the 5th paragraph of which compared with paragraphs 1 and 3, grant all buildings on estates exemption from payment of taxes, we think this doubt ought to be done away with by a special regulation, for the purpose of obviating such remonstrances which it might otherwise lead to, þÿ we therefore think that this may be done by a supplementary provision to tho first paragraph of

the above mentioned draft of law. Conformable to what is stated above, the Counthat after the last word : " annulled" in para- cil beg leave, with 12 votes against 3, to propose : graph " as regards 1 the period bo omitted, and to be added the towns," and that the following new Regulation be adopted. " The exemption hitherto granted to buildings on estates, is horeby also annulled, in as far as tbey are hired out." A minority has proposed the following amendment to paragraph 1, that after the word "an- nulled" ne added : " excepting such rooms or

houses inhabited by servants employed by the owner or the renter," in which respect it was observed, that the so called servants-rooms are of little or no use to the owners, except as abodes for servants, because the rent that might be obtained for such rooms would amount to a trifle if even possible to be collected, add to which it was stated, that the building tax is already too high, and would not admit of any augmentation ; moreover from a sanitary point of view it is considered a matter of importance, that the increased imposts should not prevent the erection of large and airy rooms in this climate. This proposition was however rejected with a majority of 1 1 votes against 3- Ad 2 we beg leave to observe, in reference to the commencement of the first period, that, that opportunity which payers of taxes are to have in order to become acquainted with the result of the measurement, it is presumed should be given to them when new Buildings are surveyed for assessment of the Building Tax as well as when Buildings already surveyed are again measured for an alteration in the assessment. The words at the commencement " If the surveying of any house or building should cause alteration in the assessment of the Building Tax hitherto paid" are therefore proposed, with 13 votes against 2, should thus be altered : "When Buildings are surveyed to be assessed with the building tax, as likewise when they are re-surveyed for a new assessment of said tax." In regard to the first part of the second period

it is remarked, that it is scarcely desirable, that the public should defray the expenses of a re-survey in all cases where the tax payer's complaint is found to be correct, since such a regulation will make the Surveyor or Inspector of Buildings careless to measure correctly, and cause expenses to the public. It will, it is presumed, be sufficient if the intent of the regulation be, that that person whose complaint is not found to be correct, shall bear the expenses of the surveying. It is proposed therefore, with 13 votes against 2, that the 2nd period should be framed thus : " In case the complaint after being duly investigated is not found to be correct, the expenses of surveying shall be borne by the person, who has made complaint regarding the previous survey." With the above alterations the draft is recommended to pass into law . I -1-1 From the Observer , July 30, 1854.

The town or village of Suiina, at the month of the Danube, is almost surrounded by a jungle of reeds, where stockades had been formed for the defence of the place by the enemy. These reeds are so high that they conceal both men and horses Irom thfe view of any one ascending the stream by a boat, and furnish great facilities for a stubborn and wily enemy to harass troops whom he is unable to meet in the field. After the capture >f Sulira last month, it was thought that the Russians had entirely left the neighbourhood, and a degree of confidence or negligence was inspired, which has terminated most unfortunately. It appears that so far from the enemy having abandoned the neighbourhood, they have never ceased to occupy the jungle which lines the banks of the river, and have wailed for their opportunity to revenge the off-hand capture of this important point. On Friday, the 7th of this month. Captain i'arker, of the Firebrand, was ascending the river in his gig, and at some distance behind was another boat of the same vessel, and Captain Powell, of the Vesuvius, in a third. The excursion seems to have been entirely unconnected with any warlike object, and so completely was the presence of an enemy unanticipated, that the captain and surgeon of the Firebrand were in the boat with their captain. As the first boat came abreast of a stockade, supposed to have been long deserted, a shower of musket balls was poured in from an unseen enemy No one was struck ;

hut a ball passed through the surgeon's coat, and one or two others narrowly escaped. The boat immediately put back to obtain the assistance of the others, and Captain Farker and his companions were disposed to treat the matter very lightly, laughing at the Russians for not being belter shots. Captain Powell with the other boats came up almost

J1 mammm , Q 'Ji 0'ISL A T 'I 3. immediately; the sailors rowed for the stockade, and Captaiu Faiker sptang on shore to lead the attack. He had made but a few steps when he was struck through the heart with a musket hall and fell dead Captain l'owell then lock the command, and in a few minutes had driven the enemy from their stronghold. The Russians, however, made a brave resistance. An eye- witness declares that the only two of the enemy to be seen at first were a coupfe of officers, who stood calmly at the embiusures of the stockade, and wete picked off by the English sailors while directing their men where to fiie. Indeed, the accounts of all our encounieis with the Russians mention the same fact, of the devotion and bravery of the Muscovite officers, who liter ally drng on their men by the collar, or force them into fire with the points of their swords The Russians seem in this respect to be exactly the opposite of their Turkish opponents ; in the Ottoman army the common soldiers are distinguished by the fanaticism aud desperation of their attack, while the officers ate bewildered with tear and responsibility. '1 he contrast leaches a kind of lesson, and shows that the Turkish resistance is that living national principle which inspired the Spaniards at Satagossa and the Transteverini at Rome; while the Russians are actuated only by the prompting of miliiary honour, a feeling seldom shared by the private soldiers, who can rise to no high rank, and must have a deeper feeling to excite them to acts of courage. The unfortu-

nate commander who fell in this affair was one of the youngest post captains in the navy; he had, it it said, just completed his 29ih year. He was the son of Admiral Hyde Fa ker, late one of the Lords of the Admiralty.
