PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL. Second Session. The 1 3th Meeting of the Council wss held on Friday the 14th of July at 11 o'clock. Absent were Messrs. Arnesen, Moore, Mc'Cutchin, Heilbuth and Castonier. In this meeting was continued the first discussion of the Draft of a municipal law The views of the Committee were fully explained by the Reporter Mr. Hanschell. Mr. Birch stated bis dissenting opinion both with regard to the Draft as well as to the report of the Committee. His proposition that the Policemasters should have seats and votes in the Burghercouncil was opposed by Messrs. Stenersen and Newton. Mr. De Gout mentioned several supposed defects in the position of the Burgher Council of St. Thomas. The meeting was adjourned at 4 o'clock.

The 14th meeting of the Colonial Council was held on Saturdav the 15th July at 11 o'clock. Absent were Messrs Brandt, Mc'Cutchin, Castonier and Heilbuth. The Chairman bad the three following final Reports read, viz : that on the Ruilding Tax, that, on Ijotterics, and that regarding marriages among the countrv laborers Whereupon the Council proceeded to the first discussion of the Draft of a. Law on an Extra Tax to be levied in St Thomas on account of the Cholera Epidemic. The majority of the Committee recommended the draft in its essontial points and its opinion on this matter was further explained by the Reporter of the Committee Mr Stenerson, who urged that under the then existing circumstances, and as the disease appeared suddenly and unexpectedly, the contracting of a loan, was the only means of procuring the money required to defrav the expenses for the sick, and that the inhabitants of St. Thomas were in general inolined to have the loan covered by theExtra Tax proposed. Mr. Riise on the contrary defended the views of the minority, according to which the loan should he repaid hv strict economy in some years, as the most natural way' and not hv imposing any Extra Tax, which in reality would prove to be a burden more for the poorer class than for the wealthy. The Governor having expressed his opinion on the matter, the discussion was continued by the two above named Committor -members as well as Messrs. Dc Gout and Hawley ; Mr. Hansohell likewise stated his opinion with regard to the

erroneousness of such assessments in general. Mr. Birch recommended the assessment of the Tax, as the. matter had been strongly recommended by the Burgher Counoil of St, Thomas This discussion was closed at the request of four of the members The meeting was adjourned at 4 o'clock

The 15th meeting of the Colonial Council was held on Monday the 17th July at 1 1 o'clock. Absent wore Messrs. Mc'Cutehin, Stenersen and Castonier. The Draft on Transmissions by post was put to the first discussion. Mr. Hanschell was the reporter of the Committee. The meeting was adjourned at 1 o'clock

The 16th meeting of the Colonial Council was held on Wednesday the 19th of July at 1 1 o'clock. Absent were Messrs. Mc'Cutchin and Newton The draft regarding an Extra Tax for St. Thomas in consequence of the Cholera Epidemic was introduced for final discussion. Messrs. Stenersen and Birch especially were in favor of, and Messrs. Hanscliell, Hawley, Riise and De Gout against the draft. At the voting, it was rejected by a majority of 9 votes against 6. The final report of the Council will be communicated hereafter. The meeting was adjourned at 3 o'clock.

The 17th meeting of the Colonial Council was held on Thursday the 20th of July at 1 1 o'clock. Absent were Messrs. Moore and Mc'Cutchin. The Council proceeded to the first discussion of the draft of the Budget for the financial year 1854-55. The Reporter of the Committee was Mr. Ohsten. After several items of the Budget had been explicitly treated on by several members, the discussion was closed and the meeting adjourned at half past four o'clock.

The 18th meeting of the Colonial Council yas held on Saturday the 22nd July at 11 o'clock Mr. Castonior was absent. The Draft of an ordinance on Transmission by post was put to the final discussion, and was decided as will be seen by the report of the Council. The Counoil then proceeded to the final discussion of a law on the importation of foreign laborers to St. Croix. Mr. Arnesen was the Reporter of the Committee. This discussion was closed aeeording to a proposition of 4 members. The meeting was adjourned at half past four o'clock.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir ! " Free Discussion," stands in painful contrast The liberal tone of your correspondent, to the narrow, illiberal remarks, in respect to your article on the Immigration Bill, made Irv one of the members of the Colonial Council during the discussions. Astonished to find that such an article was permitted to find its way in the public press!" Forsooth ! As well be astonished at our having any Press at all ! Better he astonished at himself for such an illibetal, unconstitutional remark. Does the honourable member suppose that the meagre liberty of expressing one's opinion, which the Colonists enjoy, is loo wide? Docs he feel astonished at the harmless remarks of a member of the community ? How then in the name of common sense, could be advocate the liberty of the Press, at the previous Session of the Colonial Council, which it must be supposed he did, since the Bill was unanimously recommended to be passed into I, aw ? How inconsistent in him to have voted in favor of this Bill ! I, in rnv turn, am astonished, shocked to find that any one, laying claim to the honourable attribute of being a liberal-minded man, could find foo>d for astonishment at an inoffensive article in the columns of our lametoned, censor-ridden paper. Why, if we are not mistaken, the honourable member must have harder nots to crack in the expressed opinions of the other members of the Council, during the discussions; and we think, that he might, with as much

justice and good sense, be astonished at the expresssion of these, as at the few harmless sentences in question- Yes ! it must be confessed, that the prospect of our community as regards freedom ol expressing publicly one's opinion, is sad. In 1852 the Government, perceiving that the institution of populnr representation could not work well without the liberty of the Press, lays before the Colonial Council a draft for the extension to the Colonies of the l.aw of the Press, in force in Denmark. The Colonial Council "considering that" as the Report says " the lately established representative body cannot forbear that general

interchange of ideas , which can cm/y be obtained by the means of a Free l'ress," unanimously recommends the passing of this law. So far things progressed as they ought to, under a system bearing the high-sounding name of a popular representation. In 1854 we are most graciously told that His Majesty has found it unadvisable for the present to extend this law to the Colonies This most gracious Veto appears to meet the approval of all, since not a complaining voice is raised. The Press, therefore, still stands under censorship ; but thanks to our good luck, the complaint made by Milton, that the Censor might be inferior in judgment to the writer, and thus exercise unnecessary severity, cannot be said to be applicable to that Functionary who now wields the fescue of the imprimatur. Notwithstanding, however, that the Press stands under Censorship, it would appear that the censorial power is too mildly exercised to suit the liberal views of some of the members of our popular representation. Although the Council desires a free interchange of ideas, and as the only mewns to obtain this, recommends the freedom of the Press, yet we see that an attempt to interchange a few such ideas has drawn forth an expression of astonishment that these ideas which the Council declared that "it cannot forbear" should he allowed to find a place in the Public Pi ess ! ! Strange inconsistency ! ! Things certainly wear a favourable aspect. With a representation so sedulously guarded that not a single individual can gain access

to hear one word of the discussions þÿ with a report of the proceedings of this body, as meagre as the beading of a newspaper article, and published some weeks after their taking place þÿ with a Press under Censorship, and Mill being found fault with, for daring to express an opinion þÿ with all these benefits we must certainly get on admirably well. During the Session of 1,852 the honourable 3rd rn " other for Christianstcd's District, moved that the debates of the house should be open to the public. Like many other excellent motions this one disappeared nobody knew whither. 1 am very much afraid that the opinion of Sir Thomas WinningTton, expressed m the British House of Com rnons , when the intervention of Parliament was demanded to stop the audacity of reporting the speeches of honorable members, does perhaps find an echo in the breasts of some of otw representatives. "What will be the consequence" asked Sir Tnomas "if you allow these reports to go on unchecked ? Why. Sir, you will have every word spoken here by gentlemen misrepresented by fellows who thrust themselves into our gallery. You will have the speeches of this house every day jyrinted even during your session, and we shrill he looked upon as the most contemptible asse mbly on the face of the earth.'' Things progressed, however, in spite "f Sir Thomas and his clique ; and these sairne " fellows" are not ontv suffered to enter the house of Commons, but aro provided with accommodations. Dare we expect a similar
progress hete ?

In our impression to-day we lay hefore our readers the draft of a law with amendments, to procure means for the importation of foreign labourers, with which we have been kindly favoured. We would be wanting in our duty were we not to offer some remarks on the subject þÿ even though we should he gaining the displeasure of some ; yet we

3 T $ ii <D it SSL 4 ? H consider we are but fulfilling a part of I our obligations to the public. The draft proposes that for every im- | ported labourer who engages $2 to work. the first employer must pay per an I num for the period he is bound to work in the country. It also imposes a general tax of 10 cents on every acre ot land in the country, except such as is entirely useless ; and besides this the original employer must pay 64 cents a head monthly during the period of in the tract. These expenses must one con- way or the other fall heavily on an encumbered planter ; but particularly so if he engages to employ imported labourers ; arid if he is not able to defray them, in order to supply the want of labour, he must either abandon the cultivation ot his estate, or dispose of it at a sacrifice. But if he takes the alternative, and introduces novel agricultural implements, so as to economise labour, which would be less expensive than importing labourers, he would probably find that with the few he has, he would be able to carry on the cultivation of his estate more to his advantage ; and it is our firm conviction that if improved Agricultural Implements, such as are to be found in abundance and of all descriptions in Europe & America, were imported here, and task-work introduced at fair remunerative wages, the planter, without feeling so much the want of labour as able now complains of, would be better ho to take off his crop and thereby be prevented from having recourse to the rather expensive method of Immigration.

DRAFT with AMENDMENTS ofan ordinance to empower the St. Crotx Landtrcasury to raise funds to of the Expenses of the importation defray Labourers from foreign places. L To defray the Expenses connected with the importation of Labourers into this Island, the Land Treasury of St. Croix is empowered to raise loans to the amount of $60,000, on which interest not exceeding 6 per cent per annum is to he paid 2. To defray the Interest on the loans raised in accordance with the power granted in 1 as also to defray the Installments on the Capital, there shall be applied on every 1st of July, a sum of $6,000 ; to cover which expense the Landtroasury is empowered to exact, a, 10 cents on every acre of landed property in the country, with the sole exception of such land which can bo proved to be of no use or value whatsoever ; b, a premium to the Land Treasury to be paid in concluding the contract by the person who first employs the laborer, to be calculated at to $ 2 for each year in which the laborer is bound work in the Island ; c, an impost of 64 cents pr. month to be paid by the person who employs such an imported laborer, for the period during which he is bound to work in the country. 3 Should the Taxes specified under a, and b, 2 in any year not amount to $6,000 as stated above, the Deficiency shall be paid from the other Revenues of the Land Treasury ; while, on the other hand any surplus arising shall be applied to the object mentioned in 1 or to larger payments on the loans effected.

4. It is left to the Government according to the proposal of the St. Croix Burgher Council to fix the Rules for the management and appropriation of the revenues herein mentioned. The Government is to be empowered to emanate such provisional regulations which arc deemed requisite with regard to the importation of laborers from foreign places and the position and legal interest of such laborers, and such provisional enactments subsequently shall be laid before the Colonial Council for further discussion, in the manner laid down in the 6th paragraph of the Colonial Law

EXCITING INTELLIGENCE.' Brcy lonii Bombarded and destroyed ! THE BRITISH FLAG INSULTED. VnsliilfuliicM of American Gun ncry. Probable War between Great Britain and the United States, &c., &c. The R. M.C. Steamer Dee, arrived in this port from Grey Town, this morning, with despatches from that place for his Excellency the Governor, Sir Henry Barkly, containing intelligence of the total destruction of Grey Town, the capital of the Kingdom of Mogqaitia, by the U. S. Sloop of War Cyane, Capt. Hollins, after a bombardment of sevjen hours. The account we have received of the transaction is entirely divested of any particulars. From all we can gather, it seems that on the 11th instant, the Cyane appeared off Grey Town, and sent a boat on shore, in charge of an officer, with instructions to demand from the authorities an apology and reparation þÿ for what does not appear. The demand not being complied with, the Cyane on I the carriage with him a fellow passenthe return of the boat, opened her fire on the town, into which the shot and shell fell thick and fast. The bombardment lasted seven hours, at the end of which time the town was on fire in several places. The conflagration raged, until the town was rntirely consumed. The bombardment is represented as having been conducted with the most barbarous cruelty. All that camo within range was subjected to the fire of the | Americans, even dumb creatures were not spared; and i head a new leathern hat box, and threw ceveral horses fell beneath the deadly m ssiles that

were aimed at them. The guns are said to have bean served in a most lubberly manner ; and a spectator would fancy that the shot and shell were intended for the destruction ot the alligators in tho morass, so wide of their mark did they fall. To this circumstance is attributed the length of the time occupied in the attack. Amongst other matters, we are informed that tho British flag (at the Consul's we presume) was shot away. This affair appears to be a new phase in American Fillibusterism. Hitherto, the Lopezes and the Walkers have confined their marauding expeditions to the island of Cuba, and the territory of New California þÿ it on his greasy head or carry it they have not dared to disturb the tranquillity of any British possession or of any state under British protecj tion ; and, although the American Press has not been tia, its " negro King," and its British protectors and sparing of its venom against the Kingdom of Mosquiallies, Americans have kept themselves within the boundary of mere words. As long as this was the state of affairs, the British Government could afford to smile with ineffable contempt at these important ravings. But the case is altered, when we find a regu-

A T Jt & larly commissioned vessel of war belonging to the United States, proceeding, at a time when the Republic is at peace with England, and without any declaration of war against the Kingdom of Mosquitia, which is in affiance with, and under the protection ol England, on some flimsy pretext, to bombard and destroy the Mosquitian capital. Great Britain has no alternative but to avenge the insult offered to her flag, and the injury done her ally. She is bound to do it, on every principle of honor and justice. If she shrink from the task, then is her vaunted protection of the weak against the oppression of the strong, as in the case of Turkey, an empty boast. She has ships in sufficient numbers laid up in ordinary, which, with a little activity, may be soon equipped and commissioned, with which to bombard New York, Philadelphia, Boston, or any one of the American sea-ports, as a just measure of retaliation for the outrage on Grey Town. The bombardment of Odessa was an act of retribution for the Sinope massacre ; and nothing less than a successful attack on some large American seaport will teach Americans that they must abstain from attacks, similar to that on Grey Town, unless they be in accordance with the laws of nations. What aid Sir Henry Barkly will be able to afford the people of Mosquitia, we are at a loss to conceive. It would be dangerous, we imagine, to send out of the island a single company of the hand-full of European and Black troops in it, as with the example of Grey

Town before our eyes, we know not how soon we may receive a hostile visit ourselves. As to a naval iorce, we have only the Steamer Argus in Port Royal. The destruction of Grey Town concerns this island deeply. The fate of that place may be ours any fine morning that the Americans may again think tit to summarily suspend their neutrality laws, and attack us; unless we are prepared to give them a warm reception. What we predicated some weeks ago seems on the point of being realized ; and in the absence of a sufficient number of regular troops, we must procure the next be6t sort of þÿprotection organize, arm, and discipline a militia force, lest we be caught napping, and pay as dearly for our negligence, as the inhabitants of Grey Town for their refusal, to submit to the dictation of foreign marauders. We have no account of the numbers of killed and wounded in Grey Town ; and it does not seem that the Americans have occupied the place.

A Bold Stroke. þÿ We heard an anecdote from a gentleman who recently travelled by train from Bristol to London, which displays the quick-witted promptitude of some people. There was in

ger, a stranger to him, but who while looking out of the window soon after the train passed Swindon, had his hat blown off. Without hesitating a moment, or pausing a second in perplexity, he took from the roof straps over Ins

it out of the window after the hat. All looked astonished at this appearance of | foolish wilfulness, and our informant ! ventured to ask him if he thought it a wise act, because he had lost his hat, to throw away his hat-box also? "Certainly" replied the other ; " my hat was a new hat, and if some workman or policeman picks it up, he will either put along to the next station in his hand, until, on a wet day like this, it is ruined. Now, when he sees the hathox near it, he will have the sense to put it into it, and my name is on the hatbox ; so that I can have both sent up to London after me and so saying he deliberately put on his travelling cap, and made himself quite

easy on the point. Our informant, on returning from town, was curious enough to inquire at Swindon if these calcula tions were successful, and learnt it was just as be anticipated. The hat and hatbox were found, and the name being seen, they were forwarded to London for the owner. þÿ Bristol Times.

From the Glasgow Gazette, July 15, 1854. A NOBLE RUSSIAN LADY. The following lines, from the pen of Mr. William Sinclair, author of " Poems of the Fancy and the Affections, " were suggested by the subjoined paragraph from the United Service Gazette of the present month: þÿ "A private correspondent who has just left Odessa writes in admiration of the noble and generous conduct of the Countess D'Osten Saeken, who supplied the wounded among the officers and crew of the Tiger with every necessary and delicacy from her own house. Such has been the Countess's feeling for the friends of the deceased that she sent by the Vesuvius some of poor young Giffard's hair set in an elegant gold locket to his mother, and some of the late Captain's hair which she had preserved, was given to the widow on her late visit to Odessa. Her ladyship has also taken a youngster named Robinson to live at her house. Such traits of humanity make the horrors of war the more to be regretted." Though the night may be gloomy, there is still a star Like Mercy to look from the depths of the sky, And a gleam of Humanity, brighter in war, May tell us of Love and Divinity nigh.

Confusion and danger, and dreadful affright. Had in thunders rolled over Odessa I ween. And the horrors of shipwreck had startled the night, While desolale Ruin hung over the scene. Said Giffard þÿ " Lads, greet ye Old England for me !" And turned his pale face from his shipmates so dear ; Oil ! the pulse of each sailor beat high on the sea While the words went to Heaven with the sigh and the tear

Mild Pity, who mourned for the fallen, looked down. While bore they the dead and the wounded ashore And a gleam of celestial compassion was thrown On one heart ere thy sufferings, young Giffard, were , o er ! " Oh, Love !" said the Countess, " is stronger than war, And what though we fight with the lords of the sea ? One lock of his hair, weeping widow afar, Shall be thine þÿ and one ringlet, kind mother, to thee."
And gently were parted the locks of the young, And gently were parted the locks of the brave, And soft were tho accents that fell from her tongue, As each to her silent attendants she gave

Oh ! peace to brave Giffard, who nobly hath bled, High Honour for ever be graved on his sword '. And this lock, that hath graced the calm brow of the dead. Be it kept for the iioart he hath loved and adored " Let this ringlet be set in the finest of gold, A soothing remembrance of danger and woe, To his mother the boy was a treasure untold, And 'tis meet his memorial should speak of it so "
Thanks þÿ thanks to thee, Lady ! thy feelings reveal The love and the sympathy dearest to fame. And Britain can honour, as Britain can feel, The kindness that taught thee Humanity's name.

To the Editor of the St. Croix Avis. Sir ! Permit me through the medium of your Gazette to make a few remarks, in the hope of deriving information on a subject of some interest. In the month of July 1853 the Guadeloupe Lottery Tickets were introduced here, and purchased with avidity by per- | sons who were under the impression that the drawing would take place on the 18th day of December last as stated on the tickets, and as a large surplus of the Fund which would arise from the to them the original Share, will realize that amount , ; sale of tliese tickets, was to be appropriated to the building or rebuilding of a church in Guadeloupe, the project was encouraged in this and the other Colonies, and hundreds of persons purchased them in the hope that they were facilitating a laudable purpose, and that a reasonable proportion of them would be entitled to a reimbursement resulting from an impartial drawing. In consequence of reasons, which were not made known to the holders of these tickets, the drawing did not take place at theappointed time; hut was postponed to the 29th June last, and when that period arrived, the drawing was again deferred, although it was stated in a French Colo-

nial Paper that it would positively take place on the 29th June without further postponement. I have not heard of any satisfactory reason being; assigned for the postponement of the drawing, and having sold a great many tickets, and being interested in a large quantity that is deposited in Banks tor safe keeping, I feel desirous to know to what circumstance is attributed the postponements that are a foundation of various surmises, and am also desirous to be informed whether the drawing will ever take place. Presuming that the circulation of the "St. Croix Avis" extends to the French Colonies, and thinking it probable that this number may reach Guadeloupe, I trust this portion of its contents will not be unworthy the notice of those who preside over the Lottery affairs, and flatter myself that they will respond to it in a manner that will be satisfactory to me and the pubjic in general. I am, Mr. Editor, Respectfully

LEG ISLATIVE PROCEEDINGS To the Honourable The Colonial Council d-, \c-i <5'c By Joseph De Gout, 2nd Member for St. Thomas No. 6. A Bill representing the abuse attendant on the executing of laws, without securing the means to enable the Magistrate entrusted with their administration, to observe the scale of penalties in proportion to delinquencies or crimes; and recommending the Building of a Gaol which will offer the means of correction corresponding with offences against the public peace and morals. 2nd Session. There are no establishments in the Town of "Charlotte Amalia" in St. Thomas, calculated to supply the purpose of a common Gaol and House of Correction. The absence of such an institution augments the catalogue of evils, ex.posed by the non-existence of various public edifices, conducive to the general interest and security of the Community. The practice of accumulating ordinances, imposing penalties, renders it also indispensable to provide the means for over, their faithful execution and consequent efficiency. The neglect of these precautions is on anomaly which displays the serious defects of Colonial Legislation, either in regard of the public officer on whom the responsibility devolves to watch over the public weal, or the degree of protection due to criminals or delinquents. In the first case, the Magistrate compelled to act without the means which correspond with thi grade of crimes, cannot be held responsible to public opinion or legal þÿordeal the po-

sition in which he is, placed tacitly admits of a discretionary power, although inconsistent with the limits of jurisprudence ; nevertheless the abuse or neglect of that power ts beyond the pale of coercion inasmuch that his independence of action is unquestionable, owing to the peculiarities of the disadvantages

3 'jr» 0 Jt 1 1 £ i'tts stated. In the latter case, the awarding of penalties, disproportionately to the degree of delinquencies is an evil which cannot he defined by the plea of the want of means to modify the decision of the Magistrate; such a plea is overruled hv the truthful axiom that the conviction of the injustice of a sentence, disproportionate to the degree of culpability, effectually destroys in the mind of the party subject thereto, the acquiescence of the necessity and propriety of the punishment, an acknowledgment not only useful to society, hut also of vast moral influence towar s the promotion of the feelings of practical reform among the vicious ! If it may he affirmed, that contingencies of tins kind have occurred, or nre perhaps of frequent occurrences, that ordinary delinquents have been taxed witli penalties inconsistent with the nature of the offence þÿ a decisive reply could he made. Place within the power of the Magistrate the means which are indispensable to the legal execution of the law and improvement of society, and then, only then, exact the responsibility which will naturally devolve on that functionary and the natural influence that the baneful effects of judgment exceeding the limits of crimes will be averted. These objeots cannot be ob tained without the means recommended in the Bill. 1st, The establishment of a common Gaol and House of Correction, subject to the various regulations namely: þÿ where it is their 2nd, A hoard of inspection for the same.

This system has been thoroughly discussed and adopted in other countries and the beneficial effects are generally acknowledged. In illustration of the necessity of adopting' the object recommended in this Bill, the following statement is submitted to the Council, wherein will he found such facts as will naturally attract its attention to the importance ot the subject. Fort Christian in St. Thomas. Locality of the place of confinement for Prisoners and sanatory condition. Locality. That portion of the premises devoted to the confinement of prisoners or cri- , ininals does not correspond with the requirements of a prison þÿ consequently could not have been erected for that purpose. , 2. There arc only 11 cells þÿ nine of which are allotted to civil and ordinary prisoners, and two to parties confined as debtors. Unadopted for the purpose of a prison, it is not surprising to observe, the many disadvantages and inconveniencies of the cells, as well as the imperfect means of ventilation þÿ hence the peculiarity, not only offensive hut prejudicial in tropical climates þÿ morethe probable injurious effects on the health of the garrison in a contiguous situation. Notwithstanding the limited extent of the cells, it appears that on several occasions, from 40 to 60 prisoners have been at times confined; such a course is highly objectionable, considering the remarks already set forth, and it would he interest ng to ascertain the extent of the mortality among the parties who,

after having been corfined, have been sent to the Hospital in consequence of diseases possibly contracted during their incarceration. regtmen. The regimen of the prisoners is uniform, that is without any variation, and consists of Ordinary Prisoners. In the morning one biscuit and a moderate quantity of sugar and water

Breakfast, Corn Meal and Herring. Dinner, do. do. " do. For each ration 13 cents are charged 1 Seamen. Morning, Tea and Bread and Butter. Breakfast, do. do. do. Soldiers. For this 20 cents are pharged ' Dinner, the same as is allowed to the Discipline, Health, and Morals. JVo distinction appears in the mode of confinement, beyond the separation of the sexes, nevertheless, youthful delinquents are indiscriminately confined with aged criminals, hence the chances of contamination are positive1 No attention is bestowed in regard to the clothing of the prisoners þÿ if in rags, they are allowed to remain in that state, nor is there any particular time set apart for the bathing of the prisoners, as a pre cautionary measure against diseases ; when discovered to he offensive they are ordered to do that which should be enforced as a rule at least every week ! No evidence exists of the intention to improve the, period of incarceration by the useful and successful admonitions to delinquents and criminals, in accordance with the system in active operation in the Colonies. The prisoners in St. Thomas remain, however lengthy the period of their confinement, debarred from any moral or religious admonition þÿ they are never visited by any of the Clergymen residing in that Island, consequently the valuable agency of the Ministers of religion, in that sphere duty to act, is lost to society! Nor does the King's Physician, whose inspection is necessary to provide every sanatory means, visit the

cells but when especially sent for by the Police to attend on anv of the pri soners who may be ill ! These facts are sufficiently powerful to justify their statement to the Council, for the purpose of recommending to the notice of the Government the necessity of a Gaol and House of correction in St. Thomas, and meanwhile, the organization of some efficient rules towards the amelioration of the discipline and regimen of the prisoners, in conformity with the prudence and good order indispensable in the management of similar establishments. JOS. De GOUT.

Disagreeable Collition at (ireytown. From thrPortof Spain ( Trinidad) Ga:.,July22 The unwillingness or tardiness of the British Government to fulfil the conditions of the Clayton-Bill wer treaty lias had deplorable consequences. The English Consul continuing to claim jurisdiction at Greytown a number of Americans removed to the opposite side of the harbour, and there founded a settlement, to which they gave the name of Aspinwall. Animosities between the rival parties continued, however, to increase, and the result may be gathered from the subjoined extract of a paper published at Aspinwall, and the depositions at the coroner's inquest. The newspaper article may be regarded as the American, the depositions as the English version of the affair. Great local excitement, it is obvious, exists. It is for the governments at London and Washington to prevent these private feuds from growing up into national alienation. The question seems not to be so much whether the Americans hate acted wrong, as whether the English, by remaining where they had no right to be, have not given occasion for the quarrel. England has no interest in occupying Greytown, and her representative at Washington long ago agreed that it should be evacuated.

From the Aspinwall Courier , May 23. On Tuesday afternoon last this quiet city was thrown into an intense excitement, by a rumour reaching here that one Antonio Paladino a citizen of Grenada, while coming down the river in his hungo, was ran into and shot by Captain S. S. Smith, of the steamer H. L. Ruth, also on her passage down, filled with California passengers. The facts, as far as I can learn, are these The þÿ steamer Ruth, on her down trip heavily laen the river being low, in passing over a sand bank, broke both her rudders, and thus became almost ungovernable. In passing the hungo, the steamer ran into her, and in consequence of a hostile feeling existing between the parties some altercation ensued, during which Antonio seized his gun, and pointing it towards the steamer, attracted the attention of the passengers who informed Captain Smith of the offensive manifestation. Captain .Smith levelled a rifle and shot Antonio through the heart, killing him almost instantly. The body of the deceased was brought to the station house at Greylown, a coroner's jury summoned, and evidence for the people taken, whereupon the jury found that Antonio Paladino had been killed by " sn arm in the hands of Captain S. S. Smith." A warrant was immediately issued and placed in the hands of the city marshal, and an especially deputed constable, who, at the head of about 20 armed natives and a hungo, proceeded to the other side of the bay to make the arrest, seeing which, the United States Minister, Major Borland, refused the

arrest, stating that Captain Smith had been given up to him, and pleaded a want of jurisdiction on the part of the citizens of Greytown. Some wrangling ensued, when the marshal, with his poste comitatus, returned to the city and represented the matter to the authorities. During his declaration to the citizens, in an alarming state of excitement, information was given that Captain Smith and Major Borland were then at the residence of Mr Fabens, the American consul, a few steps distant. The fact being stated, the utmost confusion appeared, and application was made to the mayor for the immediate arrest of Ma- |or Borland, who told them, that in the opinion of the city attorney, " the person of a foreign minister was exempt from arrest foiled in this, a mob left the station house, armed with muskets, swords, clubs, die , and surrounded the residence of the American consul, at which Mr. Borland was stopping, and demanded the arrest of the American minister. The consul went to the door and ordered them off, which was peremptorily refused. Mr. Borland then came down, and calmly and dispassionately told them the consequences of their outrageous and riotous conduct, but to no purpose ; the crowd, in a state of great excitement, pressed upon the doors, when one of the rioters threw a broken bottle at the minister, hitting him in the face and cutting his chepks severely. Mr. Borland then immediately requested the consul to proceed to the American steamers lying in the harbour and procure assis-

tance. Arriving on board the Northern Light, a statement of the case was made to Captain Churchill, who granted permission to lay the matter before the passengers. A meeting was ; plete. called on the quarterdeck, at which some 800 passengers were present. The consul stated the facts as they had transpired on shore, and the passengers responded that they would go, demand the unconditional release of the American minister, and bring the perpetrators of this barbarious outrage to justice, Mr. Fabens, Captain Churchill, and some half dozen more, deeming it more expedient, appointed a .committee of three to enquire into the matter. On ncaring the shore, they were hailed by a party of armed men, inquiring the nameof the approaching boat. The committee responded " Northern Light." The guard then informed th.em they could not land. The quartermaster, under whose charge the boat was placed, then stated that the consul was on board, and desirous of goin.t to his own house. The reply elicited was, " He can't land." Notwithstanding this, the boa.' attempted to advance, and was fired into, upo.tl which she

. JN © <© Ji 2L ii T II put about for the steamer. During all this, time the minister remained at the consulate, virtually under arrest, no communication being permitted with him, the consul himself not being allowed to visit his own residence. On the following morning Mr Borland left the consulate and arrivad on board the Northern Light, where he was received with hearty demonstrations of sympathy and joy on behalf of his fellow countrymen. A council was then held, at which Col. Fremont and Mr. Scott, the agent of the N. T. Company, were present; and in view of the existing state of things a force of 50 men were enlisted, to be armed, quartered, and provisioned at the expense of the United States Government, to defend and protect Point Arenas from any and every encroachment of the mob in possession of the city of Greylown. The guard was placed under the command of Crawford Fletcher, of Arkansas, and still remains quartered at the Point Throughout the first two days a night patrol was placed along the bay fronting the city, and all intercourse with Point Arenas suspended. The officers of the city government have resigned their respective stations, and the city is without law. Friday morning an English steamer of war dropped into the harbour, since which the control of the place has been given up to Her Britannic Majesty's consul. Most of the citizens are leaving; some have sold out and taken the English steamer for Aspinwall. The Northern Light left Wednesday afternoon, with her as passengers Mr. Borland

and Captain Smith, with despatches for the home government. All are in a quandary as to the probable results of this barbarousoutrage, and we trust the much-vexed question and the serious difficulties in relation to this place mav now be immediately and permanently settled, and the question of title to this portion of the coast be clearly and definitively determined.

For the ''Avis." It is with great regret that we behold the natural beauty of our island so rapidly fading away, by the perishing appearance of all the cocoanut trees throughout the island. Every one who has travelled through this island will assuredly concur in our opinion ; that added to that remarkable feature which is so manifest every where in the superiority of our high roads, the continuous border of cocoanut and cabbage trees produces an effect equal in grandeur and beauty to any that the lover of nature's beauties would wish to behold. We think it is about two years ago when we first observed that the luxuriant foliage of all the cocoanut trees in the lower jurisdiction of Frederiksted seemed to be threatened with a general blast ; and this phenomenon has gradually traversed the lengthy road between both towns ; till at length it is to be seen even in Christianstod. Upon a careful examination of one of the leaves, we have discovered that the parched appearance of all the cocoanut trees is the effect of innumerable insects infesting the under surface of every leaf, so completely, as to produce a most speedy and effectual termination of its verdure, and will consequently ensure the entire destruction of each individual branch, and finally of every tree, if nothing is done to arrest their almost resistless , hold. Wc venture to express it as our opinion, that the declining state of this most ornamental species of trees growing in the West Indies, and in so great

abundance and beauty in this island, is a subject which ought to demand the immediate and particular attention of those engaged in agricultural pursuits ; for not only have the physical beauty and picturesque grandeur of the island been very greatly enhanced by the luxuriant foliage of the cocoanut tree, but much comfort has always been added to the meagre condition of the labourers, who daily r.esort to the picking of the young cocoanuts, the gratefulness of whose water is too well known and valued by all classes to require comment. If the dried nuts were seasonably gathered on those plantations where this fruit abounds, and a little economy and industry expended, we think many dollars might be added to the overflowing purses of those immediately concerned in agriculture. We wonder that the Agricultural Society never paid any attention to this subject ; but our wonder ceases when we consider that that body is defunct-, (?) and that when it did exist, its particularattention was given to the meetings at Turin's, and the best means of procuring " artificial food" for the stock ifc. We must, in conclusion, hope that the attention of those whose duty it is, will be speedily turned towards this subject, for we predicate, that in a very short time we shall be entirely deprived of all the cocoanut trees in the island, if something is not speedily done to arrest the progress of the devouring insect. A. R.

The Budget for the financial year 1854-55 was put to the final discussion, and after having been fully discussed, was decided on in such a manner as will be seen from the Council's report theroon to II. M. the King. The meeting was adjourned at 6 o'clock p. m.

The 20th meeting of the Council was held on the 26th July at 11 o'clock. I he draft ot a new Municipal ordinance was put to the final discussion Mr Hanschcll was lleporter. A number of amendments were proposed by the Committee elected to report thereon in conjunction with the 5th member for Christiansted, Mr Birch, the most of which were recommended by the Governor, and with but few exceptions agreed to by the Council. The Council also unanimously agreed to recommeud, that the draft with the proposed amendments, be issued as an ordinanco for the Burgher Councils of these islands. EKOCEEIHNU OK THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session ltc|iort lo His Hajofy On the draft of an ordinance directing that marriage shall not entitle Laborers to dissolve their contracts in the Danish Wcstindia Possessions. From the preamble to the draft of an ordinance, directing that marriage shall not entitle Laborers to dissolve their contracts in these islands, we learn, that the draft has been caused by an abuse of the 2d paragraph of the provisional ordinances

3 concerning the relations of labor on the estates, the provision of which : that marriage shall be considered a just and legal cause for removal from one estate to the other, having been applied even in cases, where the parties in question were married previously to their having engaged themselves on different estates. The intention of the draft however is not only that ol remedying the abuse in question, but that of annulling altogether the said provision, because the nature of the con- | tract demands, that married folks, if even the marriage takes place during the course of the year, ought to remain in their service each respectively, until after having given due warning, they can leave it. The Colonial Council fully agrees in the necessity of remedying the said abuse, which is contrary to the object of the abovementioned rule, and plainly offers the opportunity of making marriage a pretence for violating the contract arbitrarily without warning and at any time during the course of the year ; but at the same time the Council is of opinion, that for the present we ought not to go beyond that limit, and therefore allow the existing rule to remain in force with some modifications, so as to guard hereafter against its being abused. It is certainly according to the nature of the contract itself, that the parties concerned should be bound to remain in the service to which they have agreed by the contract, until the expiration of the year, not regarding whether

marriage is an act depending entirely on the will i gations of has the free laborers of the one of the parties to the contract. The Danish Code 3, 19, 9 and 4, 1, 37, contain however instances of exceptions from this obligatory result of personal contracts ; and likewise there are, according to the conviction of the Colonial Council decisive reasons why legislation ought not to annuli the right already granted to the estate- laborers in these islands in the said respect. The relations in these islands make it especially incumbent on the State, according to the dictates of religion and morality, to promote marriages. The former condition of slavery among the great bulk of the population was in this respect an essential obstacle ; but subsequently the exertions of the teachers of religion, as well as the influence of the School and Church instruction, and the feeling of independence among the laborers themselves, and their desire to enter into a state which, according to their already developed ideas, conveys a particular social esteem, have during the latter years occasioned, that marriages also among the lower orders in these islands have increased to a great degree, to which result also the abovementioned rule in the provisional regulations have essentially contributed. Hut it is not only from a moral point of view, llmt the promotion of marriages in these islands must be a predominant consideration for the legislation. The welfare of the Colonies, as far as regards agriculture, is in a great measure depen-

To-day, being the Jewish Sabbath, I went, accompanied by a friend, to the Synagogue in Seel Street. We discovered the temple from a Hebrew inscription over the entrance. Worship had þÿcommenced so we opened the outer as door hats reverently we entered to comply with our ideas very quietly, and took off our of propriety, as well as to conform to the opinions of decency and respect entertained by the community in : England. The door keeper, however, requested us to keep on our hats, and, opening the folding doors of the place of worship, ushered us in. We chose the lower- j most seats in the Synagogue near the door, but were invited to more commodious and conspicuous seats j near the centre of the building, and close by the desk | where prayers were being read. A gentleman gave us a book, one page being printed in Hebrew and the other in English, and ho told us to read backwards. The Jews commence all their books at what we call the last page and terminate at. what we call the first \ page. All present had their hats on their heads, from the chief rabbi to the door-keeper. The desk at which prayers were being read was on a circular elevated platform in the centre of the Synagogue : it was neatly railed in. The chief rabbi was accompanied by two other officiating priests, and he read, or rather chanted, the prayers in Hebrew in a very peculiar manner, and responses were made by the worshippers every now ana then. To all this 1 listened in profound ignorance

of the words uttered, but I was impressed with deep and solemn thoughts as I stood among the worshipping assembly of the descendants of the good Abraham, ; whose adventures I used to read of with much devout reverence ; of Isaac, who went out to meditate in the eventide ; and of Jacob, who saw in his dream a ladder set on the earth, the top of which reached even unto heaven, and on which the angels of God were socending and descending. 1 did not understand the meaning of the ceremonies, but I knew them to be part of those which were ordained by their wonderful lawgiver who was found by þÿPharoah daughter s in a cradle among the bulrushes of the Nile thousands of years ago, and I was well aware that the God whom they ! were now worshipping was the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob. One of the priests held something in his arms, wrapped in cloth, which I cannot well describe. By and bye this was deposited with much ceremony in a recess at one end of the Synagogue, which had before it a curtain, and which conrained a number of other matters. This recess was on an elevated dais, railed in, and communicating with rhe floor by a flight of steps. During prayers 1 noted down from the prayer book, which proiessed to be the same book as that used by the German and Polish Jews, the following articles of I he Jewish creed : 1 , God is the Creator and Governor | of the universe ; 2, There is one God, and one only, and he is indivisible ; 3, God is incorporeal, and there can be no similitude or likeness of him ; 4, God is the

first and the last of things ; 5, It is to God alone that we ought to pray ; 6, The prophets are true; 7, Moses was true, and exceeds all prophets either before his time or since ; 8, The law handed down to us is the true law of Moses ; 9, This law is never to be changed by God; 10, God the creator heareth all our actions and thoughts ; 11, The Creator will reward those who obey the law, will The Messiah and punish those who disobey it ; 12, yet come, though his coming lias been delayed, and we mlist wait patiently for his apat þÿGod own pearance; 13, There will time. s appointed be a resurrection of the dead This is an epitome of the creed, not the full words thereof. Seeing none before me but male Jews I had forgotten that there were such beings as Jewesses, but, iooking around me, I saw a gallery, the front of which was lattice work, and through this lattice work I saw many bright eyes peeping, and bonnets and ribbons, and other gew-gaws. In their worshipping assemblies the male and female Jews do not mingle together. After prayers one of the rabbis preached þÿ a very in teresting sermon from Leviticus xxv. 23, The land shall not be sold for ever, for the land is mine, for ye are strangers and þÿsojourners. He pointed out the beauty and utility of the them for his people, to prevent law that was made by God from setiing too much affection upon land, as well as on other earthly possessions. The land is mine, says God : it is only given you in trust for a time : you must not sell it for ever,

nr look upon it as yours for ever : ye are only strangers and sojourners upon it. So we find that the jubilee year came round every fifty years, when all land that had been su'd reverted to its original possessor. The preacher took occasion to caution his hearers against accumulating and storing up too many earthly treasures, more than could possibly be used or consumed by them or their families ; and he described an insect which was said to live only for one hour, and which spent almost all its brief period of existence in storing up food which it had not time to enjoy before it was numbered with the dead. We laugh at the folly of this insect, but do we not follow its example when wc call together too much treasure and worldly goods. The book (pointing to the Bible) should be our treasure, and the rule and guide of our life. It is full of example for us to imitate, and of rule to guide us, during our pilgrimage on earth. We are all, as it were, pilgrims journeying to another land; and we must take care not. to do anything, or to neglect anything, that would hinder our safe arrival at our destination. Many of our nation and people, we know, do undertake a pilgrimage to the land of our fathers, to Judea, that they may die there, and be buried there; but what would we say to one of these pilgrims if, after setting out, he loitered in the countries through which he passed, occupying his time with, and of spending his means upon, the gaities and frivolities those coun-

QUtQtSS Alt 2 S tries, instead of pressing forward on his journey ; and so when the time arrived for him to die ere he had reached the destined goal, his mind was filled with I remorse, and sorrow, and shame, for his foolishness. The above is from the pen of a gentleman, a native of this Island, now on his passage to Australia in the Great Britain. A. L,

OBITUARY. DIED on Tuesday evening the 29th Inst., after a lingering illness, Mr. Jens Tikjob, a native of Denmark, aged 35 years, deeply lamented by bis family and friends. Mr. Tikjob was brought up in the commercial navy of Denmark, under lite auspices of bis father Captain Jens Tikjob, so well known and highly respected in this Island. At an early period be displayed talents of no ordinary kind, which on entering the service of the commercial navy of the United States, soon brought him into notice and command of the finest vessels trading to this Island. In the most respectable employments both at New York and New Haven be continued in command, encountering some extraordinary instances of danger incident to his profession, until suddenly attacked some months ago by that illness which has now terminated so fatally. He leaves here a widow and two children, and in Copenhagen a mother and many relatives to lament and deplore the loss of an exemplary and affectionate husband, father, son", and brother. Christiansted, St. Croix 30th August 1854. A. L. ' ' 1

3 A correspondent writing from Bucharest on the 30th July, " You says : þÿ can form no idea of the brutality of the Russians to their proteges. On their flying retreat they have taken every description of cattle and provisions they could find, and have carried oflf with them all those instrumental in maintaining security and order, leaving this poor land in the greatest misery. The people remain quiet and orderly, rejoicing that these northern guests are at last obliged to leave us. I say obliged.' ' General Adlerberg, as I learn from the best instructed sources, arrived at the head-quarters of Prince Gortschakoff with despatches from his Majesty, the Czar, commanding the prince to employ every strategical means to drive the Ottomans from Wallachian ground. Gortschakoff explained to the general the impossibility of fulfilling the imperial mandate. Adlerberg arrived at Frateschti at the time that Gortschakoff was drawing up his plan of retreat. At this interview a rancorous and violent discussion took place between the two generals of the Czar. In the presence of his aidesde-camp Adlerberg upbraided the Prince with an aimless neglect of his duty, and even intimated that he was guilty of cowardice. The Prince, who, like most Russian oflicors, is very irritable, would hear no more, but said that Adlerberg being merely the courier of the Czar, his duty was to deliver his despatches, and receive the answer ; further, he had no business in the camp. To this Adlerberg, who is more of the courtier

than the warrior, answered tranquilly that he would rather ' be a conscientious and faithful courier than a beaten and retreating general.' By the interposition of an officer high in command, the two generals were apparently " Not an reconciled." armed Russian is now to be found in Bucharest. The sick and wounded, moreover, have been removed from the hospitals, with the exception of some thirty whose cases are desperate. After the unsuccessful battle ol Giurgevo, Prince Gortschakofl" had a two hours' close conference with General Budberg, and immediately after that an order was issued to remove all the sick to Fokschani and Jassy. THE REVOLUTION IN SPAIN. POPULAR VICTORY. The revolution in Spain is now to nil appearance brought to a final issue, and that long oppressed counliy may fairly he eongtatulated on having shaken ofl the yoke of a despotic and corrupt Government, and laid promising foundations of future freedom, at a minimum cost of blood. The national watchwords. "Liberty þÿ Public Order," are now triumphant in Spain. The event is welllimed, and may have an immense influence upon the affairs of the world At a moment when the fear of change perplexes monarchs, and the immense success of the Paris coup d etat of 1851 has excited the envv of wouldbe despots throughout Europe, it'is well that an example ol a diametrically opposite kind should occur, to restore the wavering faith of the believers in self government. For years Spanish freedom has been a dead letter. Successive Ministries, each surpassing its predecessor in reckless misprision of popular rights, had cut off, one by one, nearly all

8 a 'I 21 & T U the blood-bought liberties of the people. For the last three years the advisers of the Spanish Queen had cherished the precedent of the massacre ol the Boulevard Montmartre, had put their trust in military force alone, had dreamt only of coups d'etat, and had continually conspired to abolish in form as well as in substance the right of the Spanish people to govern themselves. Now it has turned out that the mere shred of liberty, left by those enemies of all freedom, has preserved Spain. While proclaiming the nothingness of that theory from the heights of their triumphal barricades, the people ought to have deposed all pretenders. The press, however, is iree, foreign journals are admitted without censure, a national guard is instituted ; national and municipal liberty is promised, and a freely-elected Parliament is to assemble with the fullest powers. May success attend this experiment. þÿ Ibid, August 6

RUSSIAN GUN-BOATS. A Baltic correspondent lias something are called to say of the Russian gun-boats: "They ' scheren flotte,' (shallows fleet,) of which the number, divided into several divisions, amounts nominally to 800, having their principal stations at the mouth of the Neva, Sveaborg, Revel, Abo, Rotschenhalm, Wasa, &c. These boats are manned with from forty to fifty men, and are mostly fiat-bottomed. They are worked with sweeps, have two long 36-pounders, one a-head the other astern; draw little water, and, as a matter of course, have a pilot or master aboard, who is thoroughly acquainted with all the narrows, inlets, shallows, and difficulties of the coast near to this station. The construction of these craft scarcely admits of their putting to sea, especially in rough weather ; but they are admirably adapted to their intended purposes, and will cause our small steamers much trouble, and perhaps some loss. Portions of the crews of this flotilla are armed with rifles, of which the Finlanders know how to make good use. The construction of these boats appear to admit of their not carrying guns of heavier calibre than 36pounders for solid shot."

DECIMAL COINAGE. A very influential deputation waited on Tuesday upon Mr. Cardwell, at the Board of Trade, to explain their views ou the subject of decimal coinage, and, if possible, to procure that right hon. gentleman's influence with the Cabinet for the promotion of its legalised introduction. The views of the deputation in the endeavouring to introduce the new system of decimal coinage were thus stated: þÿ Mr. Bennoch said that in his opinion the sovereign should he retained as the unit of account, seeing that our whole commercial transactions were based on it, and all our national obligations were represented in that denomination. He would have the sovereign represent a pound, the florin the tenth part of a pound. The farthing he would continue as a mille. But another coin þÿ a cent þÿ must be obtained to represent the hundreth part of a pound. This would he the only new coin required for decimalising our system. The value of our copper coin being arbitrary, and 50 per cent, above its intrinsic worth, the necessary change in the nominal value could, without injustice, be made by proclamation. Taking then the sovereign as the principal coin, the florin as the tenth of the sovereign, the cent as the 100th, and the mille as the 1,000th, you would have a complete decimal system. As a matter of account the change would be of incalculable value, in saving time and procuring accuracy. Being a merchant and manufacturer paying wages weekly to between one and two

| thousand people, he could testify to the great inconvenience felt from the intri- I cacies of the present system. He trusted that the Government would not wait for popular impulse in the adoption of this 1 proposed change. The matter was was purely intellectual, one in which the | populace did not take an immediate in- | terest, while it. was one of which all intellectual and educated men felt the importance of. Mr. Cardwell said that with respect to the adoption of a decimal system of coinage, he thought that the public mind should he previously prepared for it, as history informed them that much discontent had often arisen from the sudden adoption of a new system of coinage. lie thanked the gentlemen present for the information they had afforded, and thought that they could not be more advantageously employed than in prosecuting their inqni ries on the subject. þÿ The Observer.

EMIGRATION TO CANADA The progress of the British North Amen can colonies lias again hcen illustrated by returns just issued of the emigration ol the. past year, and the continuous demand tor labour. It appears that, not withstanding the current to Australia, tiic total arrivals in Canada from Europe in 1853 were only 6$ per cent, below those of the preceding year, the numbers having been 36,(399 against 39,176. Of this number 18,972, or rathei more than one-hall, were natives of Ireland, 4913 of Scotland, 3928 of England, 3135 ol Germany, and 5123 of Norway ; while the remaining 628 were from Holland, Sweden, and other places, in the Irish emigration the number of females preponderated in a remarkable degree over that of males, the difference being more than 18 per cent. This fact is attributed to the shipment of young women from the poor-unions, coupled with the extent of remittances from settlers already prosperous, to enable their wives and sisters to join them Of the entire number of 36,699 emigrants, the proportion thai remained in Canada was 25,195, while 11,504 passed through t lie United States, nearly the whole of the Norwegian arrivals having been among the latter, owing to the difficulties they experienced from ignorance of lite language, which would he obviated in the Slates by their availing themselves of some extensive settlement already opened by their countrymen in Wisconsin. Their habits of industry and general suitableness to the Canadian climate cause their departure to he regretted

About 200, however, were induced to accept railroad employment at Hamilton, and it is hoped that these may form a nucleus to induce others for the future to become settlers The emigration described in the present report refers to that only which takes place by sea. A large number of settlers arrived via the United States, the total during the past season being estimated at 5000. þÿ Glasgow Citiren

Kcport to His Majesty On the draft of an ordinanoc directing that marriage shall not entitle Laborers to dissolve their contracts in the Danish Westindia Possessions. (Concluded.) In conformity with the foregoing the Colonial Council beg leavo most submissively to recommend, with 8 votes against 7 : that the present draft be altered thus : " The provisions contained in the 2nd paragraph of the ordinances of 26th January 1849 for St. Croix, of 18th May samo year for St. Johns and of 13th June same year for St. Thomas, relative to the dissolution of contracts of labor on account of marriage, shall in future bo interpreted thus, that marriage only in cases when entered into during the run of the yearly contract shall be considered to establish the right for the dissolving of the contract, on the conditions therein mentioned, and in such cases the party who intends to move to another estate shall give notice at least 3 weeks previous to the ceremony of marriage taking place And with the same number of votes, that the title of the proposed ordinance be : " Ordinance containing further provisions relative to the 2nd paragraph of the provisional ordinances of 26th January 1849 for St. Croix, of 18th May same year for St. Johns, and of 13th June same year for St. Thomas." The minority fully acknowledge, that the promotion of marriages among the lowor orders in these islands is an extremely important object, but oonsider it to be an error when tho legislation endeavors to urge that purpose by moans of sa-
crificing correct principles. When we allow the one party alone to break a contract, then this must without doubt in course of time impart to

the unenlightened multitude slack and confused notions of the duty of keeping a promise ; and if the said privilege of the laborers actually does contribute towards promoting marriages among them, the only thing thereby gained would probably be some statistical figures. The nature of the case seems to warrant, that those who break a contract for the purpose of getting married, even if so doing they act under the law, cannot be expeoted to consider matrimony more sacred than the oontraot which they broke. And if this cannot be expected from those who break the contract for the purpose of getting married, it can still less be expected from those who get married for the purpose of breaking the contract, and the number of the latter is proportionally perhaps not quite inconsiderable. Generally speaking it may, in our opinion be surmised, that a sound and christian moral is the only safe foundation, on which the promotion of the above important aim can be built, and in consequence nothing is gained for the morality of the common people by these marriages, for the solemnisation of which the privilege in question would be an essential condition.

It is a fact, that marriages among the country population have inoreased very much since the emancipation ; but the causes of this fact must probably be looked for principally in the entire spiritual development, which the abolition of slavery introduced, and in the greater influence of the school and of the clerical instruction since that time.

The said privilege relative to removals has doubtless not been any essential co-operating cause, and in as far as it has altogether had any effect, it would surely be better that it had not. Acknowledging the promotion of marriages to be an important object, involves the acknowledgment that matrimonial cohabitation is a condition But here we must not lose sight of, that the amount of what in this respect might be brought in question, in by far the greater number of cases would only be, that the parties concerned would work at different places for a limited period during day-time, something whioh happens everywhere where the laboring class desire work, and which system it can scarcely be important to connteract here by artificial means. That the laws contain instances of exceptions from the obligations inherent on personal contracts, could at any rate only be considered of any consequence, in case ratio legis were the same as here. Moreover the matter, from the point of view which here ought to be taken up, is more of a moral than of a mere juridical nature, and, if even exceptions altogether alike could bo pointed out, they would not justify that the law in the present case should sanction an exception from a correct principle, when it was not evidently necessary or expedient. From what has heen alleged above, this cannot be acknowledged to be the case. It would on the contrary appear, that by the said provisions in paragraph 2 of the provisional labor-regulations the law has entered upon a wrong course,

from which a complete return ought no longer to be delayed. That this should not be practicable without causing discontent among the country population, would in all probability be an unfounded apprehension. It would be proportionally quite a small part of this population, on whom an ordinance in conformity with the draft, would immediately be applicable, and fixing of a proper time from which it should come into operation, would at all events remove any valid reason for complaining of a change which in itself was beneficial and just. In accordance with the above, the Minority most submissively recommend : that the draft be most graciously approved.

We perceive from the St. Lucia Palladium of the 20th August that Cholera has been committing fearful ravages in that Island, atyl up to that date Ei.even Hundred persons had fallen victims to the Epidemic þÿ this number is said to be one twentieth of the entire population. Accounts from Barbadoes state I hat the disease in the Country districts is on the decline; but in the Parisli of St. Philip it rages yet to a fearful cxtenl. The Epidemic has now appeared in St. Vincent. The Barbadoes Liberal of 6th August states: "the disease was said to have broken out in the Carib county, either on the 8th or 9th instant þÿ for the account is not very clear on this point; and when the report reached town on the evening of the 9th, there had been five cases, three of which had terminated fatally up to that time. The account goes on to say, that the disease was supposed to have been introduced by clothes brought from St. Lucia to be washed." The accounts from Grenada are still very distressing.

The "AVIS." Christiansted , Friday the 8th September 1854. The law containing provisions for re- 8 gulating a O the relations between Masters and Servants in these Colonies, which was put in force on the 1st April last, is provided with many important and beneficial clauses. One of the principal or most important, illustrating clearly and binding as it were, all the other clauses of (lie law, is this one which enforces the procuring of servicc-books for servants and the presentation of the same before the Magistrate for legal entries when servants obtain service. This feature of the law is, doubtless, looked upon by some persons as mere formality; but we believe it is strenuously carried out by the Authorities, who have hitherto felt the want of that local knowledge so indispensably necessary for enforcing properly the Law concerning Vagrancy. No one can over-estimate the advantages that will accrue in time to come both to Masters and Servants, from this measure, as these service-books contain many necessary elucidations. The law is, however, not binding on servants employed before the 1st of April last ; and consequently a few are now without these books; but within a short time no doubt all will he furnished with them; as these servants will either have left their former service and enter into new contract, or when the utility of service-books is better known, take themout themselves voluntarily. We would advise both Masters and Servants to adhere strictly to this rule ; for upon reflection

it is not only calculated for the benefit of the servant with regard to the payment of his wages and all other rights ; hut also for the interest of the Master in securing a due performance of the contract entered into by the servant; and in short it tends to check the vagrant principles so common among servants.
