OK THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session. ICcporl lo Hi llajcKly On the draft of Law containing modifications of the ordinance 25th May 1S04, concerning the Westindia Upper Court. From the preliminary remarks to the draft of law relative to alterations with regard to the ordinance of 25th Slay 1804 concerning the Westindia Upper Court, which have been communicated to the Colonial Council, we learn that it is occasioned by the necessity of retrenching (he State Treasury's cxpenccs for the Islands under the present relations, on account of the prosperity of the Inhabitants being considerably reduced since tho emancipation, and in consequence of the difficulty of paying the taxes being increased, besides which the revenue leaves a deficiency to the State Treasury. During the discussions of this matter in the Colonial Council, it has been pointed out, thai considerations of retrenchments ought not to be predominant where the question touches on the establishment of so important an institution as the superior local tribunal of the Islands ; hut the Council beg leave to observe in this respect, that it considers the arrangement of the Upper Court proposed in this draft to be answering the purpose better than that organisation of the Court, which according to the royal rescript of 4th Fe-

bruary 1820, existed until a few years ago, and also better than the present organisation ; furthermore that, as regards institutions of this and similar nature, however desirable it would be that they should attain the greatest perfection, yet the financial point on which depend the means of approaching such an aim, cannot altogether be kept out of view. By the said rescript (see the printed collections for 1820 p. 44) it was resolved, that the office of the Chief Judge of the Upper Court should be connected with the office of Juridicial Counsellor in the Royal Westindia Government, on condition that the latter office should receive annually 1000 Rd. D. W. Cy. from the fees of the Upper Court, and that the office of first Assessor in the Court should be connected with that of Dealingraaster in St. Croix Accordingly by the former of these regulations the office of Chief Judge was joined to the office of a superior Magistrate, the latter forming the principal office, in such a way, that in making appointments to the joint office administrative ability would have to be regarded preferable to independanco and superior juridicial skill, at the same time direct access was given to the influence of the executive power upon the Upper Court. This combination of the two offices did not cease before the abolition of the Royal Westindia Government Council which took place in 1849. According to the second provision of the Rescript, the first Assessor of the Upper Court, in conformity with

the ordinance concerning the Dealing Court of St. Croix dated 6th December 1799 paragraphs 6 and 7, has been placed in a relation towards one of the inferior Judges, hardly consistent with his own situation as Judge in the Upper Court, and the irregularity of this arrangement has even been augmented during the latter years by the Dealing Court suits having been made appealable to the Upper Court It has been alleged, that the organisation of the Upper Court established in the Mother Country as well as that existing here, is based on the consideration, that the Upper Court, being composed of several Judges forming one tribunal, will in some degree guarantee that the sentences of the Lower Courts are subjected to a thorough, complete and independant investigation ; but the Colonial Council would in this respect observe, that, according to the ordinance of 20th January 121 paragraph 10 it must also be considered a principle, that the Upper Court should consist of men presumed to possess greater knowledge of law than what is exacted from a Judge in the Lower Courts, and if it even could be deemed desirable to have in the Colonies a superior tribunal here consisting, as in the Mother Country, of at least some more members than what are required for passing sentence on each single case, say at least of 5 members provided the resources of the Islands did render it possible, and provided i lie want of business in the Court did not from another point of view make it completely absurd ;

the Colonial Council must decidedly be of opinion, that forming the Upper Court by the appointment of a single Chief Judge, with the qualifications that might bo exacted from an official in that situation, is preferable to the present state of things. As it now is, it constantly becomes necessary to supply the number of the members required for passing sentences, because the members in office vacate their seats for some reason or other, or are prevented by sickness or absence on leave for the sake of their health or for other purposes, so that Government must depute some Judge from the Lower Courts at times some Lawyer, or some other person as member of the Upper Court, without it being always possible to find individuals with due qualifications, and likely, during a scries of years the number of cases in the Upper Court in which sentence has been passed by the actually appointed members has i been the smallest. It may also be remarked

a t» Sf 3$ t> 3 SI AT a tfiat there is no great probability that for the appointment of an Upper Court in these Colonies, consisting of several members, many be found who possess that general experience and knowledge of those existing relations from which cases in Court arise, without which the so called Juridical erudition is not sufficient. Generally speaking it must be kept in mind, that the number of private law suits, and other cases of consequence that arc referred to the Upper Court for sentence is very inconsiderable now, and that out of the appeals of public suits a no small proportion may moreover be considered as temerarious abuses of the royal placard 23d May 1840 paragraph 1 and the ordinance of Oth January 1852 paragraph 5. But what under existing relations makes a local Court of appeal important and indispensable, is the security to the public and the beneficial influence upon the Lower Courts, that is to say, upon the acts of the respective officials which must attach itself to the certainty, that their conduct and treatment of the suit or the case in question can with case and within a short period be subjected to the investigation of a superior tribunal, the more so, as publicity, which in so high a degree compensates formal guarantees, is here but little developed. But this influence upon the general administratives of justice and what thereto belongs is essentially independant whether the superior tribunal, other relations being equal, consists of one or of more

members. The Colonial Council therefore entirely coincides in the opinion expressed by it in 1852, that in the appointment to the Upper Court of one independant Chief Judge, fully as much security would be obtained with respect to the administration of justice as by the present institution (sec proceedings of the Colonial Council 1852 No. 9 p. 73), and therefore, while acceding to the reasons stated in the preliminary remarks to the draft, for preferring this arrangement to the other therein mentioned combination of a Chief Justice and two of the Judges from the Lower Courts in the Islands, we would assign particular weight to the reason therein pointed out, that one Chief Justice filling alone the office of the court towards the Supremo Tribunal of the realm, as well as also towards the public opinion, have the entire and actual responsibility for the sentences passed by him, which is not the case with any individual member of an Upper Court composed of several members, except occasionally when a dissenting vote is given. It is not superfluous to mention in this place a consideration, which heretofore at times has been started on the question of a change with regard to the Westindia Upper Court, viz: that this institution in the colonics has a peculiar significance with respect to their political constitution, or as it is expressed in the former Danish Chancery's letter of 16th November 1839 (seethe printed collection for 1839 p. 377-378), that the Upper Court " must be an important counterpoise against

abuses of the authority," and "in this way is of essential moment in the constitution of the colonics at large, which cannot be dispensed with without pernicious effects."- The connexion meanwhile goes to show, that these arrangements were aimed against a total repeal of the Court, or against such an organisation of the same, that it would no longer remain an independent institution, but they can scarcely be applicable, when the question merely is of a retrenchment of the number of its members, and even if we were allowed to surmise that the court would always consist of 3 independent and politically uninterested jurists, the abovcmcntioncd considerations, would now be of value, for on account of the less practical development of relations since the emancipation, and especially on account of the great pretensions of the lower classes, the question is not likely to be about official abuse of power. Moreover it must be observed, that in as far as the Upper Court formally might be considered of some politi-

cal moment in the constitution of the islands, this is now become superfluous, since the Colonial Law has introduced other and more effectual guarantees, and especially in the 5th paragraph has pointed out in what manner grievances are to be represented, with regard to the manner in which the laws are maintained. As regards the special items of the present draft the Colonial Council have nothing to observe, and especially we agree with the Government, that the business of the Recorder's Office be placed under the charge of the Chief Justice, in such a mauner however, that writing the protocols of the court be performed by a clerk appointed by the Government, and that the management of the records for landed property in the Island of St Croix for the time being remains with the Upper Court. PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session. Report to Him Mtajeftty On the draft of Law containing modifications of the ordinance 25th May 1804, concerning the Westindia Upper Court. (Concluded.) Only with respect to the 5th paragraph we find occasion to propose as an amendment, that the word: "saavelsom" in the Draft paragraph 5 be altered to " og i Saerdeleshed," for the reason, that the said authorisation for the Governor, as mentioned in the paragraph itself, is given already by the ordinance 20th April 1825. pose : that the word : Referring to the above we beg leave to pro- " saavelsoin" in the 5th paragraph of the draft be altered to : " og i Sserdelesh'ed," and that the Colonial Council, with 15 votes against 2, beg leave to recommend that the draft with the abovementioncd amendment to be made a law.

A minority of two members has not considered itself justified in acceding to the provisions contained in the draft of law, which according to its opinion are in opposition to an established fundamental principle in the Danish law relative to the organisation of the Upper Courts, which principle as regards these colonies has already been pronounced in the ordinance of the 31st March 1755 paragraph 4. The minority is of opinion, that this matter ought principally to be viewed from the point of a well weighed administration of justice, and that these Colonies with a superior tribunal for civil and criminal cases, organised as proposed in the draft, would stand singly among the colonics of the other states, where cither the organisation of the Courts of the Mothnrcouutry is throughout introduced or regard has been taken to the nature of the population, and to that character which it necessarily demands that the institutions of Justice in themselves shall possess in regard of a well weighed and impartial distribution of Justice. The minority cannot acknowledge those reasons alleged for the inexpediency of the present organisation of the Upper- Court, and is of the opinion, that the inconveniences pointed out will occur in a 3till higher degree if the Court is filled only by a single Chief Justice, on whose personality it will moreover entirely depend, if it will have the esteem and confidence of the inhabitants. The minority in referring with regard to the position of the Upper Court to the Royal Danish

Chancery's letter of 16th November 1839 to the commission then appointed in Copenhagen to report on divers matters relating to these islands, hopes that the Government in deciding on this matter will consider, in how far it would he proper to introduce so important a change in the present state of transition, and moreover to the relations in the colonies, by which the mind is so easily influenced, and to that portion of the population, in number the far more predominant, which is not represented in the Colonial Council, and which is just that part of the community that, more than any other class is subject to the action of the tribunals, and to which class people in the colonies are apt to consider it necessary, that examples he shown by a quick and strict administration of justice. The minority thinks, that that security which is insured by a humane and just treatment of the laboring class and a good organisation of the Courts, will enable the Government, at a period, not far distant, in other branches to establish retrenchments, that will counter-balance those contemplated in the draft, and thus disrccommends it being made law. Thus we render this most submissive report.

Her Britannic Majesty's Ship Calypso, St. Thomas, 15th June, 1854 Sir, þÿ I have just observed the fort at the west point of the harbour fire three shots at the English ship Fanny on her leaving the harbour ; the first shot fired having struck the ship, and the last two being fired after the ship had hove to. 1 have the honor to request you will explain to me the occasion of this proceeding. Government House, St. Thomas June 15, 1854. Sin þÿ I have just received the following ex planation from the Commander of t he Fort þÿ receipt of your Excellency's acknowledge that according to the statement of the officer on guard, it had been reported to him from the guard on the battery, that an English ship was going out of the harbour without having cleared out, and as the officer, upon examination, found that only an American, Gut no English ship had cleared, he in consequence signalized the battery Prince F'rcdcrick (at the west point of the harbour) to stop the ship, and that thus the occurrence is to be ascribed to the circumstance that the ship had at her clearance erroneously been stated to the fort as an Ametican. Considering the circumstances of the case, I have in the mean time caused a legal investigation into the matter, upon its different bearings, by a military court of inquiry, the result of which I shall likewise, as soon as obtained, have the honor to communicate to you, and in the full expectation of that this

Government House, St. Thomas, June 17th, 1854. Sir þÿ The circumstances in connexion with the accident which occurred to the English .Ship Fanny having been investigated, and the case decided by a Coin t Martial, it is evident that the signal given by the Officer on guard at the Fort to the Prince i rederik's Battery to stop an English Ship soiling out of the harbour originated in an erroneous statement made by a clerk of the Captain's consignee's, he having reported the vessel as American instead of Englisti at the customary expedition of the clearance at the fort Thus, the Officer at the Fort finding no English Ship having cleared, acted according to duty in ordering the stoppage of the vessel It is not unlikely 1 hat the primary cause of the mistake of the vessel's nationality might have arisen from the circumstance of the ship having had the American flag flying from Iter fore-lop, while in the harbour. The Corporal in command of the Battery did not intend to strike the vessel with the 1st or 2nd shot, but fearing that he should not lie able to execute his order, as the vessel might soon be out of range, which before has happened, he would fire the warning shot as close as possible. Unfortunately owing to the stale of the guns or a maladroilness, he struck the vessel, and in consequence the Court has sentenced him to 1 j month's imprisonment. You are already acquainted with that 1 have caused the amount of five hundred dollars, the damages estimated on this occasion,

paid to the British Consul in behalf of the Captain. I beg you will accept the expression of my sincere and grateful regard for I ho straightforward, equitable, and at the same time, friendly mariner in which you as well as II. B. M. Consul have met me on this unpleasant occasion. It has really been an untoward event, and an object of my profound regret, which 1 beg leave to reiterate, hoping at the same time that the corresponding leadincss and frankness on the part of this government to settle the matter according to reason and justice, as it ought to bt between friendly nations, will obliterate all unpleasant reminiscences of the unfortunate occurrence. I have the honor to be, Sir. Your most obedient humble scivnni. II II BERG To Captain Arthur Forbes, 11. B. M. frigate Calypso.

PROCEEDING OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL .Second Session. Report to IIIm Ilajesty (In the draft of an ordinance extending to the Danish Westindia Possessions the Placard of 12th September 1828, prohibiting the introduction of foreign Lotteries in Denmark. The Colonial Council fully concur with the Government in the necessity of extending to these islands the placard of the 12th September 1823 for prohibiting the introduction of foreign Lotteries, and we beg leave to suggest, that the prohibition be made even more extensive here, in order that its intended object may be completely attained, on which point we intend to offer our proposals. Hut when the draft, while forbidding the introduction of foreign Lotteries in these islands, holds out the prospect of establishing a general Lottery here, for which purpose, as mentioned in the motives to the draft produced in the Colonial Council, it is intended to establish collectors here for the Class-Lotterv in Copenhagen, we must positively dissuade the adoption of any such plan. The pernicious results of the present traffic in Lottery-tickets are evident, tending as it doer, to ensnare the minds of (lie lower orders by allowing them to seek for happiness where happiness lr seldom found. While it must be acknowledged, that the welfare of the community and its existing in a civilised state is dependent on the labor and judici ous activity of each individual in his respective þÿsphere, while by promoting instruction, it is endeavored to train youth to application and order, and to seek the fortune of life in religion

and advantageous activity for the sphere in which every one is placed, þÿ while by establishing Savings-banks it is intended to encourage the lower orders to economy and to increase their savings as (heir condition is improving, at the same time an allurement is held out to tlieni, that they may without trouble obtain a greater fortune and happiness by gambling their weekly or monthly m vings, than they would otherwise attain through a lifetime of industry and order. Where an evil has spread so far, it must be the duty of the State Government to endeavor to counteract it, not only by prohibitions alone, but also by convincing the people of the justness of the prohibition, and that it tends to their own benefit. If wc prevent foreign Lotteries, and at same time establish a Lottery at home, one of the following alternatives must ensue ; þÿ either that the home Lottery must satisfy the gambling propensity of the players to the same degree as the for-

eign Lotteries, consequently not only offer just as high prizes, and be drawn as frequently as these, þÿ (but under this supposition the homelottery will lead to the same, or if drawn in these islands, to yet greater corruption than the foreign lotteries), þÿ or the home-lottery must be based on a more limited plan than the foreign lotteries, particularly with regard to the frequency of the drawings, but then, especially it also drawn at a distant place, it would not satisfy the players, and they would think themselves wronged by the introduction of a new monopoly, which, þÿ although lottery gambling were considered to be not so pernicious but that the public itself might promote it, þÿ still would prevent them from investing their money according to their own choice, and to seek their luck, where they expected to find it most easily. Besides, if an independent lottery were established in these islands, then, in order that it might offer prizes somewhat sufficient in comparison to those of the foreign lotteries, it must be based on collections in the neighboring colonies, aud thus a breach of justice and equity according to the principles of reciprocity would be committed, by prohibiting foreigners to collect here, we at the same time collecting from theui, which would naturally soon give rise to prohibitions on their part, and thus the plan would bring on its own dissolution. Wh en it has been advanced, that it would not be possible to stop the spreading of foreign lot-

tery-plans only by prohibitions and fines, but that the propensity of the players must at same time be satisfied by a home-lottery, the Colonial Council are of opinion, that an absolute prohibition under penalty aud a strict maintenance of the same on the part of the authorities, acting at the same time on the public mind, would iu a great measure check the present evil ; and at any rate it is better to obtain the point in view incompletely and gradually, than to introduce a similar evil in order to counteract the first We must therefore disrecommend the adoption of the 2nd paragraph of the draft. On account of the manner in which the traffic with lottery tickets is carried on here þÿ (a regular collection for the account of the lottery-establishment is not usual, but generally the parties concerned sell tickets, purchased for them or consigned to them, at a higher rate, sometimes by sh res of half quart- or other fractional-parts, or plans based on the division of a ticket into a number of shares arc carried about for the signatures of those who will take a chance) þÿ the Colonial Council beg leave to propose, that sueh traffic be brought under the penalty of the first paragraph of the draft. In our opinion the minimum of the tine, considering that it will accordingly be applicable to the sale of a single lottery-ticket,, ought to be reduced to $2, but the maximum, t hut may be applied for carrying on such traffic on a large scale, also in cases of repetition, ought to be

An anti-slavery conference was held on Tuesday last, at the Manchester Athenseum, at which resolutions strongly enforcing the necessity of the immediate and total emancipation of all slaves were agreed to. Mr. Absolom Watkin presided. The preliminary resolution, which was unanimously agreed to, was, that all persons who believed slaveholding to be a sin, and immediate emancipation to be the right of the slave and the duty of the master were eligible to be members of the conference. Mr. George Thompson denounced slavery in eloquent and impassioned terms. Ho reviewed the struggles which had been made since 1807 to procure the abolition of the slave trade, and stated that it was an English woman, Elizabeth Heyrich, a member of the Society of Friends, who had first called public attention to the duty of abolishing slavery. of Lord Thompson then alluded to a remarkable speech in llroiigliam (then Mr. Brougham) in 1830, which Mr. he made a withering denunciation of slavery, and characterised as a wild and guilty phantasy the notion that man could hold property in man. That expression, said Mr. Thompson, became from that time the watchword of the anti-slavery hosts. Mr. Thompson proceeded to notice the agitation which ensued on the subject, and referred to the favourable results of the emancipation of the slaves in the West Indies, quoting high authorities in support of his position. The speaker, after commenting upon a recent leading article in The Times upon the subject, contended that the re-

sults of the great measure of emancipation had for ever settled the question of the safety and practicability of immediate emancipation. Mr. Thompson concluded by proposing resolutions expressive of the joy of the friends of human freedom in commemorating the 20th anniversary of the abolition of slavery iu the British colonies, and the conviction of the meeting that the results of emancipation had been generally of the most gratifying and Satisfactory kind. The resolutions were agreed to unanimously. A resolution was then adopted unanimously iu favour of the immediate, total, and universal abolition of the slave trade. The afternoon meeting of the conference was commenced bv Mr. G. Thompson reading resolutions to be moved as the basis of the discussion which was to follow. These resolutions expressed a friendly and fraternal disposition towards the people of the United States ; but strongly denounced the maintenance of slavery in some of those States, and particularly deprecated the idea of the acquisition of Cuba by the United States, as it would lead to the establishment of an extensive American slavo trade between the slave-breeding Slates of the continent and the newly-acquired island territory. The resolutions also gave the opinion of the conference that the nefarious designs of the slave power of the United States would be most effectually frustrated by the immediate and entire abolition by the Spanish authorities of slavery throughout Cuba, and the establishment by

wise and Christian laws of the black population in the enjoyment of that liberty and those civil rights, the possession of which by the people of at the large has ever been the best and surest guarantee independence, security, and happiness of any country. Several speakers, in allusion to those resolutions, referred to the evils which they had witnessed in America as the consequences of slavery. Tiie Aland Isi.es. þÿ These isles, w Inch lie hardly 25 miles distant from Stock- " Ahvenommaa," consist by holm, and are called of about three the Finns groups of inhabited antl 200 uninhabited islands. The inhabitants, who number about 15,000, are of a healthy and cheerful race, who support themselves partly by agriculture and the breeding of cattle, partly by fishing and by acting as pilots. Thev refuse to he called either Swedes or Finns, hut proudly call themselves Alanders; and the chief island, with a superficies of about seven square leagues (while the whole group of Aland contains, they call perhaps 110 square In the "Continent." leagues), olden times it had its own kings, and supported almost half the population of the whole archipelago. In addition to many good ports, it possesses in particular the safe anchorage of Ytternaes, which is capacious enough to admit the whole Russian fleet, on the shore of which lies the strong fortress of Bomarsund, capable of containing within its walls 60,000 men. Bomarsund has only been built about 20 years, but the history of this group of islands goes further hack. Already, in the 14th century, it is mentioned as an earldom, and at different times it has been in the possession of Swedish princes and queens, whether as fief or as jointure. Up to the year 1722 the islands were used by the Russian fleet,

(which then continually threatened the Swedish shores) as a place of rendezvous. Many Alanders who had fled to Sweden returned after the peace of 1727. In 1742 and 1808 the Russians again took possession of the islands, hut the Alanders secretly organised themselves in the latter year, surprised the Russians, and took the Russian commander, Major Neidhardt, prisoner. In 1809, however, the islands were taken again by the Russians, and since then have remained in their possession. On a lonely red granite rock lie, close to the sea, the ruins of the once strong castle of Castelholm, which was up to the year 1634 the residence of the Swedish governor of the islands. The passage between these islands, with their deeply indented bays, is more like an excursion on a lake than on the open sea. It is seldom possible to see far, either ahead or astern ; the view is either hounded by fresh, green meadows, with short-legged cattle and sheep feeding on them, by nice looking villages, surrounded by kitchen gardens, or by hare, desert cliffs of red granite, abounding in felspar, among which there stretch hazel shrubs, or thin, stunted woods of pine. At one of the most easterly Aland islands, Sattunga, the steamer which plies between Stockholm and Finland remains at anchor during the night, hut at the very first dawn of day in summer it cautiously continues its course through the labyrinth of islands, the channel between which is marked out by stakes, till it arrives at the mouth of the Aurajoki, where one

lias the first sight of the shore of Finland. The Cold Water Cure. þÿ A few days ago, a party of young men were enjoying what they termed a "drinking spree," at a public-house in Market Rasen, when one of them, a wood-dealer, who had become, or more probably pretending to have become, about "half seas over," feigned to have lost a five pound note, and sent for two constables, whom, on their arrival, lie directed to search the persons of the whole company for the note. The search was soon accomplished, hut without finding the note, it was now suggested that the wooddealer himself should also be searched, and the constables accordingly commenced stripping him, and, on examining his watch-pocket, found the note. The whole company, one and all, now agreed that something in the shape of a cureative should he administered to this false pretender, in order to prevent a repetition of any similar unpalatable joke, when homoepathy was suggested as being very effective ; and accordingly the patient was conducted to a pump, and placed in an advantageous position for receiving the cooling element, which was freely applied until he exhibited signs of contrition for the joke he had so resolutely attempted to plav off upon the company.
